utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It appears the technical problems have been remedied and we are now able to start. Mr. Churcher, if I could remind you of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence, which is still applicable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Churcher, I've been asked -- it's my fault, not yours -- to ensure that we have a gap between questions and answers so that the translators and the recording can keep up with us. So let's try to remember that. Okay?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This one point from yesterday, I want to make sure I have it clear. When you were working in Tanzania on the indigenous miners project, is the name of the company you were employed by Tanzania company, KK?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a Kenyan company, KK. KK Security.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. When we left off, we were just talking, and I just have a few more questions about how you prepared your report in this case. And we were talking about drafts. How many drafts were there?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So that's the one we have, is the sixteenth draft.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, version 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When you sent drafts to the Defence, did they comment on the drafts you provided them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I only sent one draft to the Defence. The rest were for my own internal use to track changes. And after that we had a telephone conference, but it wasn't directly about the report, only that they wished me to continue and to expand, and that was in about January.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me yesterday, by the way, about what reports I'd received, and of course in fact they are on the back of the -- the reports I'd received in effect are all listed here at the back of the report, because if I received something, I'd commented on it. So largely it was Mr. Coo's report, which I was commenting on, and one or two others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I see. So there's not a list on the back of your report but all of the reports and transcripts you received, you've commented on in the body of the report.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: All that I received before I wrote version 16, I commented on in the body of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: All -- specifically actually the back of the report, as you'll see, under various headings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's clear, then. Thank you. And just if you know, did you receive complete transcripts and statements, or partial copies?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't know, but I assume that the majority of them were complete. But some were in different formats. Some were translated formats. Some were direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when you got those, were you directed to any portions which the Defence thought were particularly relevant?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Then when you speak on page 6 - it's paragraph 1 of your report - you probably don't need to look at it for this question. You say: "In reading the papers of the Fatmir Limaj case." Is that referring to all the documentation sent to you by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be referring to everything I'd seen, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hadn't seen anything from anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Just one quick question: Before their arrest, had you met any of the three accused?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And the Defence asked as a courtesy --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, you should have a packet of possible new documents. And this packet was provided to the witness at the end of his testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And have you had a chance to look through the documents?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What I want to ask you about first is your relationship, if any, to Shirley DioGuardi. Do you know that woman?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've met her twice, talked on the telephone with her perhaps three or four times over a period of many years, and she forwards me e-mails occasionally with articles of interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And she is one of the directors, I suppose you would call it, of the Albanian American Civic League in the United States.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When did you first meet her?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We first met briefly at Heathrow sometime in the late 1990s, but I -- I'm afraid I couldn't say which year. I didn't meet her again for some very long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you have any type of professional relationship with her, or is this just a social relationship because you're both interested in Kosovo Albanians?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The latter would describe it exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Are you still in contact with her?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what about her husband, Joseph?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've met him on the same occasions that I met her, but on both occasions they were not for any form of substantive talks. We said hello, had a coffee, nice to meet, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And are you generally in accord with their position towards the problem, I'll call it, in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I wouldn't describe myself as "generally in accord," no. As you know, there are other organisations interested in Kosovo, and I remain in contact with many people, but I wouldn't describe myself as "in accord," although I haven't opposed her on anything particular that I can think of.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to ask you about the document which is behind tab 2, the record of hearings before the Committee on International Relations in the House of Representatives, and these hearings were chaired by Congressman Henry Hyde. If we go to page 52. This is testimony by Shirley DioGuardi. And she states on the record: "And by the way, for the record, with your permission, Mr. Chairman, I would like to submit a statement from Bob Churcher, who works for the British Foreign Ministry, formerly head of the international crisis group in Pristina on this very issue. His contention is that most Serbs will actually not return except to sell their homes and leave." And then it continues. And on the following page, we have a short report or letter by you entitled "The Solution for Kosovo Independence." And --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, when did Ms. DioGuardi ask you to provide this information?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging from the date on the letter, I assume it was sometime in April, but I'm afraid I don't know particularly. This letter is simply a slight rewrite of something I'd done probably two years before for the International Crisis Group following the publication of a small book by the Swedish committee on independence for Kosovo, Conditional Independence. She asked whether she could use something and I said yeah, I'll redo that for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And I should say these hearings were on May 21st, 2003, and your letter is dated May 4th, 2003. I just have a couple questions about your letter. In the first paragraph, towards the middle of the first paragraph you state: "The cry of the United Nations and Europe has been 'standards before status.' This has really been interpreted as more rights for the remaining Serbs in the province. However, this is unlikely to happen yet when those Serbs were recently both dictators and oppressors and might well be so again if the province is returned to Serbian rule." Do you still stand by that statement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that, I'm reflecting the views of Kosovars, not my personal view.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, the statement says flat out these Serbs were recently dictators and oppressors. It doesn't say "in the view of Kosovar Albanians."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, possibly I should have included that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you can see the political thought there, that if people don't like being ruled by somebody else, they're likely to try and push them out so they don't get ruled again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So you didn't mean to say that the ordinary Serbs living there, many of whom are now refugees, were all dictators and oppressors, I hope.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you know, towards the end of the Kosovo war, almost all Serbian adult males of military age were engaged in the security forces in one way or another, and that of course was likely to cause problems with their Kosovar neighbours when they came home again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you mean to say by this what it says in the plain meaning, that these Serbs -- the Serbs living in Kosovo, which is what it's talking about, were recently dictators and oppressors, or did you not mean that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I meant to say is that their Kosovo neighbours, or many of them, probably a majority, would view it that way. We're talking about how to enable Serbs to come home here, not my personal opinion of who Serbs are. I've got a number of Serb friends, including Serbs from the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But isn't that -- you say perhaps you should have written it differently. Isn't it a bit reckless to put a statement like this in something which is going towards congressional hearings on Kosovo which states that the remaining Serbs were dictators and oppressors?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking back there, I think you're -- you're bringing out one interpretation which is not one that I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let's turn the page, the top of page 54. "The sensible way to solve this problem is to make Kosovo independent, perhaps all by strong safeguards for minority rights." Now, "perhaps"? Do you think that's optional, strong safeguards for minority rights?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, that's steering a balance between the Conditional Independence book and Kosovars' demands for immediate independence, and you have to read this paper in context for the context at the time it was written. And I assume that a number of people would understand exactly what I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't completely understand your answer. What balance is there where strong safeguards for minority rights are not important?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could also equally have said "of course with strong safeguards." I'm afraid I wasn't necessarily choosing that precise word "perhaps," anything other than as a conjunctive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would please ask Mr. Churcher to stand closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My personal opinion is that there should be strong safeguards while I was writing a piece.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Churcher, could you please -- and maybe the usher could assist. I want you to be comfortable -- the microphones need to be closer to you in order for the recording to pick up. At the bottom of this page, you write: "There might seem to be an obvious solution by exchange of creating two real states, Serbia and Kosova, where people actually want to live together, but Europe is of course utterly against any form of border changes." Now, that sounds quite strongly as though you're advocating ethnically pure states.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, I'm advocating mixed states where people feel secure because they know who rules them. We've seen conflicts in the area of what is now Kosova since 1913, on and off roughly every decade, and I think it's about time we found a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's right. But Ms. DioGuardi introduced your report for the proposition that the Serbs don't really want to live in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment, regrettably not of course after the events of 1998 and 1999. No Serb can make a living there. There simply aren't jobs for anybody, Kosovars, yet alone Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. So your position, then, is that no Serbs want to live in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not -- not at all. No, I certainly haven't said that anywhere. What I was inferring there is that Serbs of working class age who need jobs and want to bring up families and send their children to school have considerable difficulties. And so far UNHCR's experience has been that returning Serbs have sold the houses they've been given and moved off.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Have you spent any time talking to Serb refugees from the war?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've spent a great deal of time talking to Serb leaders and Serb refugees inside Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You haven't heard them talking about their only wish is to go back to their houses, farms, place where is their families have been for generations in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Particularly older people, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Further down page 55 -- let me just continue with the sentence and I'll let you explain it, the next sentence: "It has gone so far --" speaking of Europe, "as to use enormous pressure and threats to keep Serbia and Montenegro together, despite it being obvious that there was a majority of Montenegrins who wished to separate and quite a number of Serbs who would be happy to see them go."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And your meaning there is --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. You'll have to phrase that question more carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What exactly do you mean by this sentence?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking in the context here of the European Union idea that if Montenegro and Serbia would separate, that would automatically create the conditions for Kosovo to become independent. That's not actually a view that legally I would share but it is a view and you would possibly be familiar with the phrase "Selanija" which refers to the idea of keeping Montenegro and Serbia together as some sort of Yugoslav entity. I was saying there that my experience in Montenegro and in talking to Montenegrins at the time, the government there, was that they wished to separate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the Serbs would be happy to see them go; that's your position?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many Serbs would because of the economic burden of keeping Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In the next paragraph you state - I'll slow down - "UN agencies are of course well known for exaggerating numbers elsewhere in the world, since more numbers mean more resources and more money for the UN." Well, when you were working in Timor, did you exaggerate numbers, exaggerate problems to get more money?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't working on numbers in Timor, to I wouldn't have needed to. But it's a continuing source of conflict between WFP and UNHCR as to registrations, and registrations have always been an extremely difficult problem, which rather naturally people doing the registration tend to err on the high side because to say no to somebody is much more dangerous than saying yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. But again, isn't this a rather recklessly broad statement that UN agencies exaggerate for more resources for more money? Isn't that a bit irresponsible to put in this type of document?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then in the next paragraph: "Most Serbs who are thinking of returning to Kosovo" -- in context -- "are planning to coming" -- it should be "planning to come back to get grants to rebuild their houses in order to sell up and leave. Those who remain are the social cases."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you've travelled widely in Kosovo, you would of course observe that, as a matter of fact, on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outside the traditional enclaves such as Srpska where a viable community remains, in other areas people have left. It's not viable for them to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And the whole point of this document is to help Ms. DioGuardi convince the Congress that the Serbs don't really want to live in Kosovo, they don't really want to return there, they're just coming back to try to rip off the system.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Rip off the system" is far stronger than I would have intended to say, but if you wanted to follow that up, there have been a number of papers published recently which have confirmed that. The Lausanne principle, for instance, the recent paper on the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the only people who want to remain are social cases; there aren't any people who want to remain because that's where their families are from and that's where they were born?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said "most," not "any."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. The next document I want to show you is behind tab 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Which starts off, Your Honours -- I found this on the website over the last weekend, so the first pages you see are the cover on the Albanian American Civic League website. The last three pages are the letter posted there. And the link can be shown on the cover pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You read -- did you read this article last night --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- by Shirley -- let me finish the question, please, Shirley DioGuardi, "Kosova: Breaking the Silence"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is dated March 11, 2003, so that's round about a month before you provide her with your report to provide to the Congress; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You need to speak up a bit. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I won't go through this entire article, but it's really an editorial, isn't it, commemorating and reflecting on the fifth-year anniversary of the terrible events in Prekaz and the Jashari family.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What I want to look at is the second-to-last paragraph. It's on page 2, where Ms. DioGuardi writes: "If we are to keep faith with the Albanian heroes like Adem Jashari, then we have to vigorously oppose all attempts to misrepresent Kosova on the world stage as a pretext for carving it up and I think there is no better place to begin than to impose the criminalisation of the UCK and the recent indictment of Fatmir Limaj, Haradin Bala, and Isak Musliu by the War Crimes Tribunal in The Hague. These men have been charged with crimes allegedly committed before the war. Bowing to pressure from Serbia and its allies, The Hague is creating a false parody between the UCK freedom fighters struggling for the liberation of a people and a Serbian war -- and Serbian war criminals who committed state-sponsored terrorism, occupation, and genocide. We must educate the west about this travesty of justice and we must also expose the Albanians who have collaborated in these arrests." Now, isn't that a disturbing statement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. I haven't read this piece before. I looked at it and thought, This is probably some sort of fund-raising speech in the American style, trying to exaggerate for the sake of emphasis to get money. But it's certainly not something that I would have agreed with. And that's all I can say about it. I didn't write it. It's not part of my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the term "collaborator" has got a very grave and special meaning in Kosovo, doesn't it, in the Albanian community?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly does in the propaganda of the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you didn't feel the need to check a little more into Ms. DioGuardi's views published on the website at this same time that you're providing documentation for her to use in her advocacy?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I explained initially, that document is a rerun of something I did while I was in the International Crisis Group, supporting a particular publication of the Swedish committee, and no, I didn't see any problem in publishing that publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But I'm talking about a problem of you acting through this person as an advocate for the Albanian cause at the same time that she's calling for exposing collaborators who led to the arrest of the accused in this case.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally I don't see that supplying documents to the United States Congress is acting in collaboration with anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's not what I was saying. I'm just --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I misunderstood you then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- suggesting that you have advocated -- you have act as an advocate for the Albanian Kosovar cause in this way, providing something to Ms. DioGuardi that you know she's going to use to try to persuade Congress to follow the views of the Albanian American Civic League. You know that that's what the document you are giving her is for.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trying to persuade Congress of something is a perfectly proper and legal activity. I don't have any difficulty with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you don't have any problem being associated with people who write that type of article, that type of editorial?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not associated with that person at all, in any way. Absolutely no association whatsoever. She introduced something I wrote to Congress. Anybody can do that. I don't have any difficulty with that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't get paid for it, I might add.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. The next document briefly. Let me just ask you this, talking about, finally, this topic of the document which you provided which was introduced in these hearings: "Do you agree with your source that you cite, Stacy Sullivan, that in the 1980s and 1970s there was a concerted but unstated effort to drive Serbs out of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't recall citing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You didn't cite that. You cite -- you list the book as a source, the Stacy Sullivan book.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "Be Not Afraid." Do you agree with that source that she makes on pages 40 to 41?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that statement, but I wouldn't have agreed with that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: There wasn't a concerted campaign?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just go to tab 3 briefly. This is an ECMM report, "Kosovo, Current Trends in Kosovar Politics." Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I looked at it last night and, judging by the time and some of the phrases, I think I do -- though there's no signature block on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. Do you think you wrote it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did because I can't think of anybody else who was present at the time in the mission, and as I said, it contains some phrases which are familiar to me. But I couldn't say that for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we, I'm sorry, go into private session for one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- the copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could we provide one to the witness, please. And I should say for the record that what we're looking at is R0057722 through 24, an ECMM report from January 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you look at the last page, sir, and can I just ask you if that's your signature.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember writing this report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't, no. If I'd remembered it, I'd have told you so immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I mean now do you remember, now that you see your signature?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly accept that I wrote it. I mean, I don't remember writing it, but I accept that I wrote it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Just two questions: At this time, in 1995 - if you'd look at the last page, Section E - you're of the same view, aren't you? "E: Lastly comes a possibility" -- and here you're forecasting possible future events -- "which comes in most conflicts of the FRY realising that it simply cannot afford the cost of police and army repression in Kosovo and that basic facilities like new schools and hospitals are lacking due to the cost of holding a province where few, if any, Serbs actually want to live."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that was your view, then, in 1995. Here it's not most; it's few, if any, actually want to live.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the census figures, 1971, 1981, 1991, if you watch the declining trend, most Serbs moving out of Kosovo. It was a fact at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But, again, don't you think that's just a bit -- a bit of a broad brush for the topic, a bit reckless to say "few, if any, actually want to live" when in fact there were thousands and thousands of people who wanted to live there, who still want to live there, who happen to be of a Serbian or Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But as a percentage of the total that was dropping at all time. Old people were staying and unfortunately younger people were moving out to get jobs. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And that wasn't, again, because of any concerted campaign to drive them out in the 1970s and 1980s. You disagree with Stacy Sullivan on that point.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Didn't see any concerted campaign. I never believed in one. It's the normal economic pressures of moving through rural areas to cities, jobs and factories weren't being created. There wasn't the money to do it. Yugoslavia was collapsing after Tito's time. It was a trend.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to ask you now some questions about your views on the KLA's structure -- military structure in 1998. On page 4 of your report, you describe in the summary section: "The KLA of the late 1990s as being composed of disparate groups with different sources of support, different political opinions, differing allegiances, although perhaps with shared aspirations, but without any coherent or effective command in the military sense until perhaps rather tenuously after the war." And "after the war" means what, June 1999?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: After June 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. And you address the General Staff in your report. On page 5 you say "it is perfectly possible to see more than one General Staff." On page 6, paragraph 3, you state: "There is no concrete evidence of the existence of such a group or of the location of it."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And on page 27, you state: "If there was a General Staff in reality, as distinct from a series of disconnected numbered individuals and a mythical title." You cite the Selimi interview on page 27 of your report. Now, are you aware that he testified that he was on the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you cite Krasniqi on page 30. You've read his testimony. You know that he says he was on the General Staff. I'm just letting them catch up. And you realise that both of these men and all the other testimony in the case and probably all the documentation that was provided to you by the Defence says that there was a General Staff and there was only one General Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. Would you allow me to explain that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In a minute. There's been evidence that the General Staff in this case has been based for a time in Divjak. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And there's been evidence that the General Staff moved around for its own security.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And Mr. Limaj has testified that he was a member of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He probably knows a bit more about the General Staff than you do.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure he does.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you can explain, I think it's fair --if you've written several times "no General Staff" or "several General Staffs" or -- yeah, I guess that's it. There's either none or several. You can explain what you meant by that.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Staff back in 1998, certainly to an outsider, was not at all clear. Later on it became apparent that there might be various -- I can't really describe it well in English -- but circles within the General Staff. But the General Staff was a political organisation along the lines of a Politbureau. It was not a military command structure in the way that you or I would understand a military command structure. Certainly in 1998, it consisted of a number of individuals. As you will also see from Limaj's testimony, which wasn't available to me at this time, he didn't distinguish between representatives of the General Staff and members of the General Staff. He himself, as quite an important person, didn't know what was going on on the ground at the time. In that sense, it's difficult to see a General Staff in what people interpret as the meaning of the word, which is some sort of all-encompassing military command structure. What you've got is a series of individuals in different places at different times who come together in groups of two or three; a number of them set up in Divjak, and that is actually unknown even to the people in the area immediately around them, 10 kilometres way in Klecka. Well, that's not a military command structure. Nobody knows who's in the headquarters; nobody knows where it is. So the General Staff remains a mythical concept, as I said, comprised of individuals moving around with a political direction to start a guerilla insurgency, not to provide a military command in the way that people interpret a General Staff would. Sorry, does that answer ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's fine. I want you to be able to explain where you need to. That's an interesting explanation. I want to -- since you brought it up as well, talk a little bit about what Mr. Limaj said on Day 69, here. Mr. Mansfield asked him -- "We were in June at the moment, and" -- I'm sorry, I don't have the -- I have the page reference of page 43, so this would be on the 43rd page of the LiveNote, although it's a different number in the official. Mr. Mansfield asked his client the question: "We were in June at the moment. What other developments in June so far as you are concerned and the KLA are concerned, what other things happened in June that you can recall of significance?" And Mr. Limaj answered - and it's a very long answer, so I won't read the entire answer - "As I said earlier, the meeting with Mr. Krasniqi came as a result of the concerns from what was seen in the terrain and what was going on in the terrain. The people began to come with the request to join the KLA. And they wanted to get weapons and join the ranks and they came in great numbers." Now I'm going to skip ahead a bit: "Secondly, as Mr. Krasniqi told me, almost the entire General Staff had engaged in procuring weapons because of the question of weapons was a number one question. So they were all interested in getting as much weapons as possible and arming people who wanted to get armed." That describes the General Staff engaging in a military function, providing weapons for the KLA, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It describes General Staff as apparently doing nothing except trying to procure weapons for the KLA. It doesn't describe a military command structure in the way that many people here have interpreted the phrase "the General Staff." It implies a whole series of individuals all trying to acquire weapons. That doesn't amount to any sort of meaningful command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, it was an answer to a specific question about what Mr. Limaj remembered from events in June. I'm not asking Mr. Limaj to give a treatise on the General Staff. My question to you was very simple: If the General Staff is engaged, as he said, in trying to get weapons to distribute to all these people who want to join the KLA, that's a strong military function, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's one of many military functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: A staff should be capable of carrying out many more functions than that to be an effective staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We may not need to go through this topic too much, but you agree that in the -- throughout late 1997 into 1998, the KLA was an organisation with a great deal of secrecy?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Although, I would distinguish between the periods of 1997 and 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But in both of those periods - let's talk about 1998, then - KLA members and the KLA structure tried to maintain a great deal of secrecy.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Particularly before the Jashari massacre. I think you should see March 1998 as the turning point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And there were very good reasons to maintain that secrecy.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were at the time, of course, because it was an entirely different idea -- a political idea by different groups of how they would rebel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that's why KLA members wore masks.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume they wore masks for secrecy, but I'm certainly -- I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I believe it was Ramadan Behluli testified here that they took off their mask -- that they felt they could take off their masks in June 1998?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Because at that point they began to feel more secure.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you also realise and have heard that KLA members used pseudonyms rather than their real names.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the evidence in this trial has been that many KLA soldiers didn't know each other's real names until late or even after the war.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I've heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Which made it difficult for the MUP and Serb forces to know who was in the KLA.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not entirely sure that statement is correct, but it was possibly the intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That was the intention. You -- you're not sure that's correct, that it -- you think the MUP and the VJ knew exactly who was in the KLA?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't. I don't necessarily see the connection between those things, but there's something.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that also makes it difficult during the time period for outsiders to know who was in the KLA.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because, as I said, at that particular time there wasn't one KLA. There was a whole series of armed groups all calling themselves the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In which particular time is that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That period between March and June 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, we'll -- we'll talk about that in a moment. You talk about that actually at page 9, paragraph 15. That's where you're talking about this point. You state: "They were making their own uniforms and travelling to Albania to buy their own weapons, yet these groups had no command structure outside of their own informal and consensual arrangements, and even then what they call orders were first discussed. Indeed, in the main they were mostly unable or unwilling to leave their own villages to help anybody else unless pushed out by organised Serb military or paramilitary forces. Despite their enthusiasm, they had no command structure."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's been clear from the evidence so far in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You state similarly - and I'll just run through it - on page 14, in paragraph 33: "They were little localised groups incapable of supporting each other and not in any form of military command structure."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And as I said, I think the evidence which has come out in this case reinforces my view, although I wrote that before I'd heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you're not suggesting that first -- in that first paragraph 15 that individual KLA members travelled to Albania to buy weapons, came back with a rifle -- or a couple of rifles just for their village and that was the extent of the way the KLA was armed, are you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I said, a number of groups operating in different ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But what you appear to be saying in that paragraph is that these different groups all went to Albania just individually to buy their own weapons.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's certainly what you can see in Northern Albania. There were literally arms bazaars with villagers coming across the border and starting to haggle about the price of a Kalashnikov.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. And one of the books you cite is, again the Stacy Sullivan book, about Florin Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. On page 6 she talks about how he raised personally 30 million dollars for military supplies and weapons for the KLA.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you should take both Stacy Sullivan and Florin Krasniqi with a pinch of salt on those sort of figures. Again, it's an American book published for an American public.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Then why do you cite it in your report as good for -- as -- I'll try to find your words -- as worth reading about the build-up of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the way it indicated diverse supply lines with one group being supplied by its own chain of supply, in the same way that other groups in Dukagjini maintained entirely separate lines of funding back to Switzerland. There were a whole series of different lines of supply into Kosovo, not one line which then found out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's my point, is that there was an organised shipping of millions of dollars of weapons into Kosovo. It wasn't just villagers crossing the border coming back with their own personal weapon.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you read Stacy Sullivan's book completely, you'd see that in actual fact, although they talk about those figures the numbers of weapons they talk about shipping is actually very small. And whether any of those weapons actually reached the front lines and were used would be another question entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So when she talks on page 6 about how this individual smuggled tens of thousands of weapons across the border into Kosovo, you don't consider that a large number of weapons? That's a very small number?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't consider that that was true. If you actually read his statements within the book, he's talking about individual weapons, buying two or three here, 15 there. She's writing for an audience. You don't have to take everything in these books as serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And there's no caveat in your report about that, is there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not talking about that particular thing in my report. I was talking about the precise part reinforcing the idea that each group had its own line going back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And those groups smuggled in weapons for distribution.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To what extent that happened or what extent they smuggled in weapons for their own members, I'm not clear. But I think the latter is mostly the case. People knew who those weapons were going to as they brought them in. It was much too dangerous an activity simply to be taking weapons in for general distribution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And, again, page 6, para 3: "In terms of time, there was never any effective command structure in any military sense during any part of the Kosovo conflict," in your view.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my view. That's precisely why NATO or the American government or whoever we would like to suggest did it, brought in, again, Agim Ceku towards the end to try and get some kind of command structure. If you look at General Ralston's comments to Wesley Clark, they were having enormous difficulties in getting anybody on the ground to produce any coherent answers about targeting. They couldn't do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. My question was whether that was your view, and you've answered that. Do you know which brigade Fatmir Limaj commanded?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard the number, I'm afraid, but I haven't -- I don't recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know when he became brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you know which zone he commanded?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe he commanded --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for interpretation, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was one of the leaders in the area of Klecka, which is on the boundary of about three zones or subzones. But as you'll know, the zone terminology changed during the war because it reflected one particular political party's political intentions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you what Fatmir Limaj said in this courtroom on the 24th of May. He was asked: "And you never gave orders to Luan? That's your testimony?" And his answer was -- this is Day 72, line 64: "With Luan it's something different. When the brigade was set up, it was established in August, I was his brigade commander, and from August I issued orders to him." Now, your contention is that throughout any period, any time, there was no structure, no orders given, Fatmir Limaj never gave an order to Luan as his subordinate in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the ability to give orders to one individual is not representative of a command structure. A command structure, to be an effective command structure, in the meaning of what we're talking about, requires many more things than that. The ability of one individual on the ground to tell somebody else to go and make the coffee or whatever is -- is not indicative of a military command system in the sense of what we're trying to establish here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. But if it's not one person asking somebody else to get them a cup of coffee but a brigade commander talking to a unit commander ordering him and his unit to carry out tasks, that is a form of military command.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it was, then that would be one form of military command in a very small limited area of both space and time. You need a whole system right across the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, let me stop you there because you don't know the space, time, and area of Fatmir Limaj's command, do you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of the general point. You asked me which zones. Well, it's on the border of three zones, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, you don't -- you don't know the time he was commander, you don't know the name of the zone he was commander of, and you don't know the area under his command; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I'm saying that across the whole of the KLA, to have a functioning military system and a military command system would require much more than one individual giving orders to another individual in one place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I wonder if -- I wonder if Mr. Nicholls would be kind enough to name the zone, please, in which Mr. Limaj was the commander of.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The Pashtrik zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: He was the commander of that zone, was he? Is that the Prosecution case?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He was the commander I'm sorry, I should say of the brigade, of the 121 Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which was located across the boundaries of three zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you know the AOR of the 121 Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I would ask -- I would ask for very great care if the cross-examination is going to be at this level of detail that the detail is right, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you could produce a map, I can give you what I understand roughly to be that area, but I'm not an expert on Mr. Limaj's brigade or his area of operations. I'm talking about the general command structure or lack of it of the KLA, overall.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You've read General Selimi's transcript, of his testimony here.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have, yes, but not recently. I didn't reread it last night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You're aware, then, that he testified that before he was a commander in his area at the Drenica region, Adem Jashari was a commander.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would certainly accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Selimi was appointed commander of the 1st Operational Zone Drenica in May 1998 by the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say so. I'm -- I'm not aware of that, but I was -- I am aware that he became the commander in Drenica for a time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would point out, of course, that Adem Jashari was not in any way a military commander, had no command of anything other than his own farmhouse, which he lost in a valiant battle for a political principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or misguided attempt, depending on your view.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would also point out that Sultan, Sulejman, a young man, no previous military understanding or knowledge, trying to assume a position which he knows nothing about. He has no idea about what a commander is supposed to do. He has no idea of military command systems. It was not until Ceku [sic] came in that anybody explained to him what a staff was supposed to do. You can't simply say that by assuming a title or indeed calling a disparate group of fighters a brigade makes it a brigade in the military sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, actually Selimi did have one year of military training. I'm not sure if you're aware of that.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You may well be right, yes. He may well have done a conscription. But conscription as a private soldier in the Yugoslav Army is hardly likely to prepare you for a military command system.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I agree. And that is the fact in many insurgent, colonial wars for liberation. Not all of the people who form up to resist have formal military training. In some cases they do, but not in all cases.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most cases, probably not. That's why they don't have command systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you make the point in your report - and Selimi testified that - there was no intermediate body between the General Staff and the zone commanders.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you're aware that General Selimi was considered a good commander, an effective commander during the Kosovo conflict.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm also aware that he was replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You're aware he had that reputation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A good fighter. It doesn't mean a good commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: After his --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: A good fighter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: After his appointment as zone commander in May 1998, Selimi testified that he immediately began to consolidate the points into brigades and he appointed commanders, i.e., he gave -- he appointed commanders to the 112, 113, 114 Brigades. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm certainly aware of the way they started to try and impose order and impose a system. But trying to do something and establishing it in times of wartime when there's fighting all around you, they were just about to lose most of the ground that they thought they had taken. Of course, there simply weren't any Serbs to take it from. And the whole thing was complete chaos. Again, they didn't succeed in establishing a command system simply by appointing people to positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, but in May --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had no means of communicating with each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In May 1998 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think there's a problem with the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It should be okay now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, in May Selimi testified that when he wasn't present, his subordinate chief of staff could sign orders for him when he was unavailable.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. But they had no means of distributing those signed orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, that's not what Mr. Selimi testified to, and I think he probably knows more about it than you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would say that Mr. Selimi very reasonably as a young man wished to put a good gloss on what they'd been trying to do, which was a constant threat throughout this conflict that the KLA would like to have become something that at the time it didn't have the time to become.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And perhaps the means could be specified, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He said he was -- well, you can look at the reference and do that on redirect. It's on page 22:31. Mr. Selimi did not recall exactly how but that all unit commanders would be notified of his written orders.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: But he couldn't recall exactly how.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, whether they were delivered, sent. That's right. Ramiz Qeriqi testified at the end of May. He was asked a question: "Q. You've testified in May 1998 that Shukri Buja came and that he was commander of the area. At that time, there was a higher commander above you and Shukri Buja. "Of course there was. We weren't there without having people above us. I said from the beginning when I came there, I came from Albania, I met with Asim Syla, who was above all of us, Rexhep Selimi, I went to Klecka with Fatmir. I went to Kroimire every time. In war this is how it is. Not everybody can do what he likes. There is a chain of command. People are not appointed at will."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And yet all the evidence we've seen is that people in effect appointed themselves in most cases. The whole situation is totally confused --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Which evidence are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The evidence you've heard so far, that "I went there. Nobody told me to go." "We discussed the orders to see whether they were good."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you're completely discounting Selimi stating that the General Staff appointed him and approved his appointment.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think it's entirely true. What I'm saying is that he couldn't, having done that, having been appointed, he couldn't exercise command in a military way. He couldn't run a military command system. He didn't have the staff, the knowledge, communications, the transportation, or anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that is based on, again, material just that you've received in this case.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was -- as you saw, I wrote that report before I received the majority of this material. That was based on my knowledge of how the campaign was being conducted, the huge difficulty that NATO had in finding anybody to talk to, the huge difficulty that ICRC had in finding anybody to talk to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm talking specifically now about General Selimi and his position in May. There's nothing in your report, in the body of your report, about General Selimi --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I discounted it, because being appointed to a position doesn't mean that you're actually producing effective military command out of that appointment. You've got a title. And it's great. You've -- you now feel on top of the world. You're really feeling important. But it doesn't mean you can command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But if you have men under your command, organised in units, you're appointing their leaders, you're issuing orders, they're carrying out those decisions, you are effecting command.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you can get as far as those men, if you can get more -- further than the immediate group around you, if you can distribute those orders and see them effectively obeyed. And I've not seen and didn't see anywhere in the Kosovo war any examples of effective tactical command in the movement of units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And when you've seen, again, you're not talking about any personal observations but something you learned later after coming back from Tanzania.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about -- if you remember, I was there on -- at a time on the ground in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And in --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And listening to people coming back into in Tirana and sitting on the cafe on the boulevard, talking about it coming backwards and forwards, people going up north, coming back; myself going up north, talking to people, talking to friends about what was going on. We were very concerned, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. This is when you're catching up, learning things on the cafe at the boulevard. I want to talk to you now about something else that Mr. Limaj Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. said on Day 69 at line 46: "Either on the way going to Drenica, both during July or June. Now, I just remembered an incident which is important and can be linked with what will be said. During that time for the first time I was able to see official officers, professional ones. It was a group of three or five officers -- maybe there were more of them, but personally I see three of them, officer who is had completed the military academy, who had come from abroad and joined the KLA, and with -- via the General Staff they were observing the terrain. And if I can say, they were in a way surveilling the terrain and every unit." He continues to describe that: "We were very happy to see the presence of these officers. I know that Agim Qelaj from that small training centre that I mentioned, since Agim Qelaj was specialised in military training, he took three or four of my soldiers. He was inspired to create an intervention unit, so he took three or four soldiers from my unit and some soldiers from other units -- this was by the end of June. So he prepared them, trained them, and sent them to Negrovce village somewhere at the Vucjak gorge, there is a place between Negrovce and" -- it's mispronounced here, "Turiqevc village which is suitable for such activities." This is Mr. Limaj talking about an event he observed in June 1998.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In June 1998?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, the General Staff is present with professional -- representatives of the General Staff are present with professional militarily trained officers from abroad."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And somebody trained three or four soldiers as an intervention unit, which implies, of course -- that's the first intervention unit that anybody has thought of or heard of. Three or four soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Stop. How do you get that that's the first intervention unit?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the tone of your voice in describing that sentence. They don't appear to have had one before. This seems to be something new, by implication.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: They're surveilling the entire territory.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this also seems to be a new event. It doesn't amount to a structure, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: They're visiting every unit.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three people, trying to get round Kosovo visiting every unit? They're -- I mean, I know what they are. They're probably returning officers from the Croatian conflict, but they don't have time to start organising things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you can tell all of that from the passage I've just read? That they didn't have time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the -- from the -- of course you can. You know how difficult it was to move around at the time, how much time it took you -- if nothing else, you've read those descriptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Moving by night, having to stay in houses before you found a guide to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, we'll get to --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They weren't moving -- they weren't using maps, for a start.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We'll get to ECMM's assessment of moving around at that time. They're selecting soldiers for an intervention unit and taking them somewhere else to train them; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three or four soldiers, he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And some from another area. So my point is this is not as you describe in your report villagers simply taking up arms to defend their individual villages, which you say.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would say this was exactly what I was describing. And by June somebody is saying, Hang on, we ought to try and reinforce somewhere if they get attacked. There's take three or four soldiers and try and train them to move forwards as reinforcements. That's the way these things develop. But it doesn't mean that you've got a coherent military structure capable of enforcing orders and discipline and so forth. Is just the very embryonic beginnings of an army which never had time to develop.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We've also looked at it, and you've stated a couple of times in your report that "The KLA did not support each other."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "But units were unable to support each other."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't have any transport. They didn't have any communications. They didn't know how to move from place to place. What happened was various groups converged on the sound of firing and saw whether they could intervene or not. That, again, is not military command or military operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That is not an unwillingness to assist other people from villages either.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say they were unwilling. I said they were unable.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Look at page 9, paragraph 15: "Indeed, in the main, they were mostly unable or unwilling to leave their own villages to help anyone else."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unable or unwilling. I mean obviously some people didn't want to move from their village. Some people didn't know where to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you've just gone back on that a bit, that they were willing to say -- to assist, you say now, if they knew there was an attack or --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said some were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you've seen that in this case. You've read Ramadan Behluli's testimony.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't recall the testimony precisely, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember him testifying that soldiers would come to assist wherever there was fighting at Carraleve or Kroimire?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. But certainly I've heard similar statements on a number of actions. But, of course, coming to assist, when they're coming from different directions, nobody's got any idea of where the firing points are or how --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm focussing --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- how to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- now on your assertion that KLA soldiers were "unable or unwilling to leave their own villages to help anyone else." Now, that -- "unless pushed out by the Serbian military." Now, that's just not true, is it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some groups, of course -- I didn't -- I didn't in any way dispute that, as I've just said. Some groups went to help. But going to help is not the same as military direction. It's not the same as military orders. Nobody actually knew where the firing was coming from. Nobody knew what was actually going on. They came to the top of the hill and looked down. Then they left somebody at the top of the hill and four of them went down the hill to see what they could do. That's extremely noble, very brave, and so forth. People got killed doing it. But it's not a military system.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is it an example of military command from a unit is sent to assist another unit?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it happened in a sustained way over a period of time, then yes. If it happens on an individual occasion, well, I'm afraid that can just be chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, there's a witness - we have to use the number for him -

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, when are we taking the break? It's normally now but should we go a little bit longer because of the ...?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You've got at the most about two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll come back then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the first break now and resume at five past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Churcher, during the break I was asked again if we could both slow down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'll try.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just a couple more questions about your assertion that the villagers were unable or unwilling to assist in other villages. A witness here, L-95, testified that he was sent - this is page 49, 4207 - to another -- to assist another unit because that territory was in jeopardy, and he stated that he was sent, his special unit, when the need was for interventions. He was asked to go and assist Celiku because the territory there was in jeopardy, and he explained that "in. Jeopardy" meant that they were likely to be attacked by the Serb forces. And the witness also testified that when he was there, he was under Celiku's command. So there we have a unit of men being sent to another area where there was a danger of combat being subordinated to the local commander. That is no evidence of any command structure in any sense to you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that might well be evidence of an embryonic start to something. I noticed you used the words "he was asked to go and assist." Not that he was ordered to proceed to point X and take part in the defence of. So -- and in your previous remarks you said they took three or four people to start an intervention unit. Well, here we can all see efforts at ideas on militarily supporting each other, but my position would remain that we have a group of young men here without any substantive military experience, no knowledge of command structures, no methods of command, no method of communication, or no workable method of communication in an emergency. It doesn't amount to a military command structure in the way that one would understand it for operations. It certainly doesn't compare to the military command structure that the Serbs had.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Or the British Army. I take that point. It was not as sophisticated as the commander structure you were in or the VJ. But those are typical aspects of command, units assisting other units when there is an elevated risk.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it happens on a sustained basis in protracted operations, then yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it happens on an individual occasion, that's a one-off. It doesn't amount to a military command structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You say on page 14 of your report - this is paragraph 32 - talking about the Racak incident up there, speaking of the KLA soldiers and how they failed to defend -- to win that battle: "All they had were weapons and a determination to defend their village. But that did not constitute a military operation." Are you suggesting that Racak was defended just by the villagers of Racak? That's what your paragraph implies.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm -- I'm aware that -- or I understand that some other people came and went and had a look at that. I'm afraid, like much of your evidence, I was relying on a Serbian account here of this particular conflict and in particular the way the sentries were smoking, there were insufficient weapons between people they found, and so forth. It again was the military operation, some villagers ending up getting killed because two sentries were smoking and nobody else was standing to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just so I'm clear, you're talking there about Serb newspaper accounts; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about what was billed as a first hand account by one of the police participants subsequently published in a Serb newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Briefly, let me tell you what Fatmir Limaj said about that day, 18th of July. He says -- this is Day 69, line 67 -- "On the first part of the next day, the 18th," setting the time, "on that occasion I met with Agim Qelaj and with Rexhep Selimi and Muse Jashari, who had arrived there at an hour earlier at the entrance of Rahovec. And at that time the representatives" -- I'm moving ahead -- "of the General Staff, Rexhep Selimi and Byslym Zyropi and Muse, they told me that they had heard for the first time about the events in Rahovec this morning. And in a hurry they came in order to see what the situation [sic]and to find the way that would take us out from the position that the KLA was in and to avoid the danger which the population was exposed."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is there a problem with the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I think I can answer that one. I'm sorry to intervene, but looking at the record, there are two different places and different times being mentioned here. On the record, it's Racak at the start and then Rahovec further down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please clarify with the witness which place and which time they're dealing with. And they're different years even, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think you've confused Rahovec and Racak, which --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm talking now about Rahovec.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let's stick now to -- well, Rahovec, 18th July: "And the General Staff, Byslym Zyropi and Sokol Bashota, they decided that Agim Qelaj should become an operations commander for Rahovec and Agim became a kind of coordination point for all those who were there." Now, that is the General Staff involved in military matters, not just political matters; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to clarify, this has nothing to do with page 14 or Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I haven't written about it. But I think your statement, again, picks out exactly what I'm talking about. "Became a kind of coordination point"? That's not a military operation.
