"A kind of coordination point"? You can certainly see what they were trying to do, but they didn't know what they were supposed to do. They didn't have that sort of military experience. They didn't have that sort of military command system. They should have taken charge, of course, of Rahovec before it ever started. Rahovec was the classic problem of a number of people accidentally going to visit their families, kicking off a battle which nobody meant to be involved in, causing great concern to everybody, and nobody knowing what to do and various people getting injured or killed as a result.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a military disaster. It had nothing to do with a military command system.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And appointing an operations commander, is that not a military function?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the event? It's a little unusual, isn't it? You usual usually do that before the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is appointing an operations commander a military function?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Appointing an operations officer is part of the staff. Appointing somebody to command an operation is also a military term. But Rahovec was the classic example of the KLA's failure to have a military command structure capable of controlling its troops. They failed to stop Rahovec from happening, they failed to reinforce it, and they failed to sort it out. It was extremely damaging. Various people were rather upset about it. But it wasn't a military operation, and there was no military command in the sense that we should understand it involved. Attempting to appoint an operations commander was a good first step, but it doesn't amount to producing a military system.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And, again, this is based on your impressions, what you gathered, in Albania and then on the evidence you've heard in this case.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rahovec was very widely discussed as to why it happened. We were all initially alarmed that the KLA should try and take a town which clearly they couldn't hold. Before it fell, people like myself understood that it couldn't be held, that it wasn't in a position to be held. It's -- again, as I said, it's a classic example of the failure of the fact that they didn't have a military command system.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to talk now about your report on page 27. Do you remember there you're commenting on the interview with Sultan, Mr. Selimi?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Sorry, yes. So I haven't found page 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The interview is at tab 6, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, referring to page 22 of the interview. Are you with me?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not yet, I'm afraid. My page has only been partially printed at the bottom and I've got the numbering ... I'm with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. This is the part that you focussed on, Mr. Lehtinen's comment about the lack of military structure and Sulejman Selimi describing here that the General Staff was on top of it, there wasn't a middle step. That's towards the bottom of page 22. You state: "Comment: This seems to confirm the nature of the General Staff -- that this General Staff was not a military structure. It appears to be well established that if there was a General Staff in reality" -- we've gone through this part -- "as distinct from a series of disconnected numbered individuals, it certainly wasn't providing effective military command in the sense of this indictment. "Overall comment: Sulejman Selimi's interview is probably the best record of how the KLA built up. In particular, the reference to boundaries imposing themselves, i.e., not being directed, to the establishment of units being reported to the General Staff, as distinct from being directed or more properly ordered by them, of the lack of arrests of prisons on the ground that there wasn't time and a democratic, committee way of making appointments as late as post-war in a totally unmilitarily way." Now, we've already discussed that Selimi was fighting Serb forces in May, June, and July 1998; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to direct your attention now to page 32 and 33 of this interview. Tell me when you get there.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got to page 32.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. At the bottom of the page: "Mr. Lehtinen: Did you have cooperation with any other of the Celiku units there, the ones that were along the tarmac road, like in Lapusnik?" And Limaj responds: "They communicated with each other, for example, the 113 Brigade, which went -- was -- which was -- which was there. They coordinated. "Q. But did you as commander, did you have direct communication with Fatmir Limaj about these issues, about the gorge in Lapusnik?" "No. We would usually get our orders from the general -- from the General Staff. They issued our orders. But normally it was communication from both sides of Lapusnik pass and there was fighting on both sides -- were taking part in it, because of course he was not obliged to give any information and I was not obliged to give him information. But there was a commanding structure that gave us our tasks." That's what it states; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you select the one portion from this document which we looked at before on page 22. You put that in your report. You tell the Trial Chamber this is the best record of the interview and it show there is was no command structure because there was no middle step. And you leave out this passage where General Selimi says "There was a commanding structure which gave us our tasks." Isn't it misleading to select just that part of the interview which supports what you want to say and leave out the rest?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are many parts of the interview which would support what I want to say, including the investigator prefacing his remarks by saying, "I know there was no military system." But this particular point reinforces what I said. He's talking about, "We got our orders from the General Staff," but the General Staff wasn't capable of producing orders across the whole of Kosovo. It once again says there isn't a military system. You have to have intermediate command levels which are capable of coordinating at the local level. You can't just say, We got orders from the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So when Selimi is saying that on both sides of this road he and the commander on the other side received their orders through the command structure from the General Staff, that means that there's no command structure and the General Staff is not engaged in command there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He couldn't possibly get orders about tactical events on the ground for coordinating with each other from the General Staff in any relevant time to have any tactical input. It isn't possible, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, how do you know that it was impossible? You state in your report that radios are not the key to communication, and you -- how do you know that the General Staff was unable to receive reports in time for it to react to any situation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a constant thread through everything which is written about this year, the period. And you know they described at one point fairly carefully the radios they had, which we all knew about anyway. They were commercial Motorolas. They have a range which is strictly dictated by line of sight. Normally it goes between 3 and 5 kilometres. If you get up on a hill, you may get better at times. But it's likely to come through broken.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And therefore it's not a means of communication which can provide an effective command structure capable of transmitting orders, imposing discipline, and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If -- sorry, my question was not about radios. My question is: Even in the absence of radios, there is other ways to convey messages within the area under the control of a rebel insurgency.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: But not if you've got to go back to the General Staff and down again. You would need an intermediate level of command to do it through. You would need a level of command which is much closer to the site of your action, just a kilometre or so behind it so you can have runners, similar to Napoleon, who did it very well with men on horseback. But you've got to have that system established.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. You need --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Really you need a system to communicate with the commanding level, but Selimi's point is that he received his orders on his side, the commander on the other side received his orders from the same command level. That is a commanding structure giving tasks to different units, different commanders who have people in turn under their command.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Selimi here is clearly from the tone of the whole interview trying to be helpful. Oh, yes, well, we got our orders from the General Staff; but in reality that's a meaningless statement. You might get orders that you're going to be a commander from the General Staff. It can't amount to a military command system capable of controlling operations at a tactical level.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And yet you've called this the best record of the build-up.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general. Sulejman's account of how things built up and how disorganised it was, I think, is an excellent record.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the parts where he does talk about some organisation or command you assume he's trying to be lying and not to be honest.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly didn't say he was trying to be lying. I said he was trying to be helpful. You have to explain to someone what a military command system means and I'm not really sure that he fully understood it at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And at that time, of course, you personally had no contact --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Although I knew him personally after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. When was that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was director of the International Crisis Group in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would propose to admit the Selimi interview, simply because the witness calls it the best source of the build-up, something he relied on. It was provided to him by the Defence and he cites it. And not for the truth of the matter in the interview but simply for the Court to ascertain the way things were chosen to be included or not included in the report. But if there's not any objection to that, I don't -- I don't press it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you distinguish it from what was put to us yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. Because the witness was here. He testified. He was cross-examined on this report -- on this interview. And it's been used as a source. But I -- I don't press it. I just think it might be useful. If the Defence doesn't want it in then -- then that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm looking to see whether there's any agitation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: No. No. No agitation at all. Just mild amusement. I'm happy for a fair approach to this. Could it be marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P246, MFI.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment, Your Honour. I want to see if something is available on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to show you now, sir, an ECMM report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is -- was included, Your Honours, in Phil Coo's report and has been referred to by the witness in his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, again, we talked about ECMM yesterday. You were in ECMM. ECMM works on the ground, travelling through areas of conflict; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This report is from the 22nd of June, and I think you remember reviewing this report as part of your report to this Court.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry? I didn't understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You've seen this report before. You refer to it in your report.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. This is an assessment of the UCK; correct? Do you see that in the heading? Can you read what's on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only read the area which has been blown up, I'm afraid. I can't read the whole report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's -- let's go to the blown-up area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: If there's a copy of the whole document, could that be given?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's -- it's in evidence. I don't have a -- a clean extra copy for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I don't mind an unclean copy for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm quite happy to accept what you tell me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll blow up the portions. This is one of the annexed documents. It may -- Mr. Hasan will find -- Mr. Younis will find a copy for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, in the introduction, which you can read, the reporter states: "We have encountered UCK on numerous occasions and I personally have been somewhat startled by the extent of their control." And then he issues a caution: "The following is, however, the product of only one week of monitoring, and our impressions must therefore be seen as essentially limited." Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, although I'm sure you understand the meaning of "control" here in the sense that this is the area of territory on which they've found armed Kosovars who say they're members of the KLA. That doesn't imply control in any military sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You agree that at this time the KLA was controlling a large area of Kosovo, 30 per cent? And I'm talking about 22nd of June.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree that the KLA was present. I would think you would have to be very careful about the word "control" since you might put implications into it which ECMM would not have meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Control" means literally finding people in the villages, as distinct from finding Serbian police in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think we've got a paper copy for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, the second heading --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you indicate the number, Mr. Nicholls. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The ERN number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it not an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It is an exhibit, but it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can we have the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's -- the exhibit is -- I'm trying to remember. It's Phil Coo's exhibit, which I think -- report, which is 220 or it's 230, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is the print on the paper large enough for you to read?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah. That's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In the next paragraph the observer states: "UCK territory. Significant swaths of the central regions of Kosovo west of Pristina are now in UCK control with Serb forces now limited to one very vulnerable main supply route south from Pristina to Prizren. Where once areas of concern such as Drenica were seen in isolation, we are close to being able to see the vast majority of an area west of Pristina as a whole. The UCK appear to control an area west of Pristina that connects Drenica to the area immediately south, centred on the town of Malisevo. Control by the UCK of the central section of the main road west from Pristina to Peja has been the key to this linkage in an area between Komorane and Kijeve which both remain in Serb police control," and I don't need to continue there. Further down at the bottom of that paragraph: "By far the most extraordinary area is situated north-east of Orahovac with the central town of Malisevo the focus of a so-called liberated territory that virtually scrapes the edge of the main peripheral road. The Serbs MSR, especially at Suva Reka." The next paragraph, "Road infrastructure." "The most striking aspect to much of the UCK-held territory described is the extent to which the UCK have utilised and improved the local infrastructure, with small roads now being used to ensure a wholly integrated territory that can aid swift movement between areas. In essence, it appears that much thought and probably more strategy has gone into the taking of this territory than most observers felt was likely." Now, that's the assessment on the people who were there on the ground at the time.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the assessment of two monitors, and I think the key to this, of course, is the phrase "than most observers felt likely." Most observers thought that this was villagers improving tracks between villages in the same way that villagers were giving their machinery out and digging trenches in highly unsuitable places. There had unfortunately been no direction to it, as was proved when the whole thing collapsed like a pack of cards the next month. There was actually no strategic ability to manage this territory. And as you saw, it collapsed completely in the VJ offence of July, which swept everything before it. This was a spontaneous rebellion of a whole series of villages who, as you say, or as they say here, linked themselves with these dirt roads. And then the whole thing collapsed in days. And once again, it almost proves that this was not a well-thought-out military operation, and indeed I from Mr. Limaj's testimony the other day he had great concerns about the so-called liberation of Malisevo, which again was shared by other observers. It was once again -- it was certainly our opinion that they weren't going to be able to hold this territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So what's happened here is at this point in time in June the KLA, according to these observers who were there on the ground, has been able to link a large area of territory -- is at this point before the July offensive keeping these Serb forces out of that territory, and have developed a way of quickly moving through the area by developing the roads. So it may not -- you may consider it an imperfect military operation, but they have found that strategy and thought has gone into creating this territory.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't describe it as "an imperfect military operation." I wouldn't describe it as "a military operation" at all. I would describe it as a series of villagers getting out their hunting rifle, send ago few of the boys back to Kukes or to Bajram Curi to try and buy an AK-47 and, in tremendous euphoria, celebrating the fact they've achieved victory only to see the whole thing collapse before their eyes at the first movement of Serb forces. We're not talking about expelling Serb forces here. We're talking about expelling village policemen who had already retreated to their police stations and were not patrolling very much in 1996 or 1997 either.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, the police fighting for the MUP, the Serb forces, those weren't just village policemen.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police before the offensive were largely village policemen. That was the MUP's problem. The MUP was driven out of just about everywhere because the MUP did not want to take risks and did not want to confront things. They were good at arresting people but they were not good at fighting for the control of territory. And you'll also see that from senior VJ generals complaining about the performance and behaviour of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And -- and asking that the VJ be given a greater role in taking back control of the territory.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And they were. And that was a military operation. We saw the results of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the other thing this observer notes when moving through the territory: "In two recent instances, the team has been escorted by UCK through the area of southern Drenica and in one instance was provided a relayed escort through territory that has become a network of connecting tracks and roads that have been upgraded through a recent local effort. What was perhaps even more significant was a level of communication between escorts that seemed to have expected our imminent arrival."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the unit. I've never disputed that there was communication at the local level. What there wasn't was an effective intermediary level of command or series of intermediary -- there should have been a whole series of nodes of command extending down from a central command which was responsible to some sort of political authority up through brigade commands, battalion commands, and so on down. The ability to liaise or coordinate, as the KLA was so fond of describing itself, between units at ground level, which did exist at times - after all, one little boy can run to another little boy - is not indicative of a military command system.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, but it shows that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the speakers to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the KLA were able to communicate rapidly with each other when necessary.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't think it showed anything more than one village knows people in the next village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's all the ECMM reporters are reporting there, that the villagers in adjacent villages know each other.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I tell you what I would see would have been a command system, then? If the night before ECMM had been able to contact a headquarters and arrange an itinerary going from village to village, that would amount to some form of command system. But simply being able to liaise neighbour to neighbour doesn't constitute one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, there have been other ECMM reports in this case. And I can show it to you if you want -- which talk about the kidnappings of four Serbs. And I can give the reference. That's R 254-4282, part of Mr. Coo's report. Including two refugees from Croatia. These were the Bakrac men. Have you heard before at all about that particular kidnapping?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard about that particular incident, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You've also -- no doubt recall Mr. Krasniqi testifying in this courtroom that he remembered that incident and that those men were in fact released by the KLA to the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Although, I -- in general, I would not give much weight to Mr. Krasniqi's statements at the time which were by his own admission largely propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you could look at P48.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is the Koha Ditore article from 12 July. U003-8586. That should come up on Sanction, the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we don't need to go through this whole document, which has been seen by the Chamber before. But here Mr. Krasniqi stated: "First of all, the Serbian forces, whether the police, the military, or armed civilians, are our enemy. From the start, we have had our own internal rules for our operations. These clearly lay down that the UCK recognises the Geneva Conventions and the conventions governing the conduct of war, even though it has not been offered the chance of signing them, as it would have done. We do not go in for kidnapping. Even if some people have suffered, these have been more Albanian collaborators than Serb civilians. We do not deal with civilians and we return those whom we take as prisoners of war. A few days ago we hand over two Serbs originating from Croatia to the International Red Cross. Those we have kidnapped are either announced on a list or reported to be executed, but we do not behave in a base fashion like Serbia." Mr. Krasniqi stated that on the 12th of July, 1998. He stated in this courtroom that it was correct about those two civilians being released. So you accept that that was not propaganda that the KLA had released those two men?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the sense of that precise line that those two people were released; I certainly accept that they were released in general. Mr. Krasniqi's statements by his own admission were part of a propaganda war, which was normal in many conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that corroborates the ECMM report of these men being kidnapped at a KLA checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure it does, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And yet you rely on the Selimi interview to state on page 27: "The interview shows that there were no arrests or prisons because there wasn't time." That's your analysis.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I deal with kidnappings at the moment in Afghanistan. It doesn't mean there was any precedents. We've simply got a case of criminal kidnap. And this doesn't mean there's anything different here. The very fact that it took several days for someone to negotiate their release again shows the difficulty of finding a competent headquarters with a capability of controlling or issuing orders or imposing discipline. We are talking about a straightforward kidnap, as we deal with in Afghanistan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is confirmation of persons being arrested, detained, and then released through negotiation; correct? Regardless -- you can call it a prison -- let's just call it somewhere where people are detained.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kidnap is a criminal offence anywhere in the world, and "kidnapping" was the phrase that you used initially, not "detained" or "arrested."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "Kidnapping" is a phrase Mr. Krasniqi used. "Kidnapping" is a phrase the ECMM used.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to be very reasonable.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no objection to that. Again, I don't see that it in any way implies a coordinated, functioning military command system which was capable of recognising the fact that people had been arrested or capable of organising their release in a timely manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. My question was why you put in your report that the Selimi article is indicative of the lack of arrests or prisons on the grounds, that there wouldn't have been time for that. You don't think that's a recklessly broad statement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've continued to make the distinction between kidnaps and arrests. I said I deal with kidnaps in Afghanistan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And on page 20, you state that "ECMM reports were largely staffed by seconded or retired military officers and that they tried to impose military order in their reports." Do you really think you can dismiss the bulk of the ECMM documentation just on that basis?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't said anywhere that I dismissed it. I'm indicating that, as with all types of reporting, you need to look at the origins of the people doing the reporting and you need to understand their strengths and limitations. Therefore, you need to treat such reports with caution if you don't know who the authors are personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So in general, then, you would give credit to ECMM reports which are corroborated by other evidence.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general, I would give credit to ECMM reports dealing with events on the ground. I wouldn't necessarily give a great deal of credit to conclusions drawn from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, your position, as you've stated, again is no command structure, no conflict until sometime after the war.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my position, yes. No effective military command structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me ask you to look at tab 5 in your bundle. That's the report that you did on Kresevo. And just to be clear, this is your report; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: From 2002?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you just tell us quickly: There's a map on page 5. Kresevo is this small area at the borders of Kosovo, Macedonia, and Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, the paragraph I just want to ask you about is just on page 1 at the bottom, where you state: "The Albanian rebels in Kresevo were and are not a unified movement. Both the Kosova and Macedonian rebellions by Albanians against Slav rule, or misrule as they saw it, were reasonably unified. Both had only one large and one small organisation involved in commanding parts of the armed rebellion." Now, you're referring there to the Albanian rebellions in Kosovo that we're talking about as well as later in 2001 in Macedonia; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You distribute it here as "reasonably unified"; correct? The Albanian KLA?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say here "militarily unified" or "militarily commanded." There was one KLA by the end of the Kosovo conflict in which by and large all believed they were part of the KLA. And I'm making a distinction here that the UCPMB had an even-less organised structure. If we wanted to go further and compare an Albanian rebellion which had a more organised structure than militarily, the Macedonia conflict demonstrated an effective chain of command on at least two occasions which was commented on. Whereas the Kosovo conflict in my view never demonstrated that chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. You describe the Kosovo KLA rebellion as "reasonably unified." You're not talking about people here, you specifically state: "The Kosovo and Macedonia rebellions by Albanians were reasonably unified. Both had one large and one small organisation involved in commanding." What were the large and small organisations you were referring to involved in commanding the Kosovo Albanian rebellion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the fact that Dukagjini did not really ever come under any form of agreement with the General Staff, although there use no open conflict but they didn't actually really recognise the General Staff in many ways. Although that's a very unclear area politically. But we're talking about political recognition here. We're not talking about a military command system.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, but you're talking about armed rebellions in this section, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the political intent behind those armed rebellions and who started them off and who came together, not any system of military command or control. I haven't used those words anywhere there that I can see, and certainly didn't mean to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, you do. You say "were reasonably unified. Both had one large and one small organisation in commanding parts of the armed rebellion." Why didn't you just say in Kresevo the situation was the same as in Kosovo; there was no command structure whatsoever, if that's what you meant?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't talking about command structures here. I'm talking about the political direction or incentive behind the creation of groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's what you mean by "commanding the armed rebellion"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And you'll notice that I haven't used the phrase "military command" and I've very carefully said "armed rebellion." And I haven't suggested this is a force. I wouldn't have agreed with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me move on now to discuss discipline. You say on page 5 of your report: "There was no system of military discipline." On page 9, para 16 you say: "There wasn't any form of military discipline."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I was working on the wrong document. Page ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The first reference was on page 5, and the second is in paragraph 16 on page 9.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I think if you read that paragraph as a whole you can see exactly what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. You're aware that Sulejman Selimi testified that "If soldiers misbehaved, their uniforms could be taken away, their weapons could be taken away, and they could be kicked out of the KLA"; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly think that's true, yes. I don't regard being dismissed from an organisation in that way as an effective system of imposing military discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you may have read in his interview at page 45 in addition that he would tell them that they could never be in the KLA again.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think I commented on that, that the ability to dismiss somebody from a unit, whilst again, possibly, an embryonic - and these are my words now - possibly an embryonic start to some form of disciplinary system, it doesn't amount to an effective system of military discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you also talk about the Kacak [phoen] tradition. And you agree with me in -- for Kosovar Albanians in these rural areas, honour is a very important thing. Defending one's honour, protecting one's honour, and not offending anybody else's honour?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. It's also - and this may be in your report. I don't remember - it's what might be called "a gun culture." Gun, weapons are important.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that's in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But would you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I wouldn't agree with that statement particularly strongly, but I would agree there are elements of truth within it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, my uncle was an RAF gunner in World War II. That was a popular war, like the KLA rebellion and war was a popular war with the Kosovar Albanians; correct? By "popular" I mean it was supported by the populace.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Under those situations - let's just say it's England - if a young man is joined up, and is kicked out and given a dishonourable discharge, we call it in the US, goes home to a small village, people say, "What are you doing here? I was kicked out of the KLA. They took my gun and my uniform and told me I could never come back." How is that seen in the village?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously and socially that's going to be difficult, but I don't imagine social difficulties are part of a system of military discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Isn't being thrown out of the military a -- a form of punishment in different professional militaries around the world?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not normally a form of punishment until after punishment has been carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, let me just -- the only thing I've found, quickly, is from the Canadian Forces, the Queen's Regulations and Orders for the Canadian Forces, Volume 2, Chapter 104, "Punishments." And one of the punishments listed is "dismissal with disgrace." That's a punishment.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my experience, that only comes on top of other punishments. It means that no one wishes to retain this person in the service because of what else they've done and because of the way they've been punished for it. Obviously the -- the difficulty otherwise with soldiers that any soldier who wants to leave the army simply misbehaves and would get thrown out. And you very rapidly have no army left if you can't be careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And to follow that, could the Prosecutor please describe the system of discipline employed in the Canadian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can't describe that and you can do that on your redirect, if you like. I can provide you with a copy of the Code, 104.08, which describes Section 141 of the National Defence Act, dismissal with disgrace as a form of punishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, did you read the testimony of Fadil Kastrati in this case?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember reading -- this is at 226, 17 to 18 [sic], about how Commander Celiku took his weapon away from him?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, the beer incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just read you a particle of it then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "To my misfortune Mr. Commander Celiku came and he asked me are you Fadil Kastrati? I replied, Yes, that's me. He said to me, You, sir, have to be unarmed. It was very difficult for me when I heard these words. I was very sorry. I was very cross with him. But now I'm convinced that he was right and I have a deep respect for him and for any other soldier of the KLA. I asked him, is it possible for you, Commander, not to unarm me? Because I took this weapon with a great will and wish." I'll skip a sentence. He said to me, It's not up to you to speak. I know when I should arm you or when I should disarm you or when I should not unarm you. You disturbed the order in the village and the discipline here. I said to him, No, I did not cause a disturbance but I just reminded that person that he should not speak too loudly because it can be -- it can harm our soldiers. Commander Celiku said to me, You have to be unarmed because there are regulations and discipline in the ranks of the KLA and for that discipline we have to act this way. And if we allow the smallest mistakes to take place, it's better that you don't have a weapon. And this was it." And then he describes how his weapon was actually taken away for 15 days. He eventually got it back after 9 days, and he said, "When I got my weapon back, I just don't know how to describe this event. It was a great thing for me." You don't see anywhere in that any form of discipline?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said before, I see the start in being able to dismiss someone or take their weapon away of an embryonic system of discipline. But without a system of control, without a system of confirming sentence, without a system of a whole hierarchy, I don't see that as anything other than isolated incidents which would not prevent someone from doing something that they should not do. I mean, let's say you're proposing to shoot somebody in an illegal way. Do you think that having your weapon taken off you afterwards is going to influence that decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that's what you mean by no -- not any system of discipline?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You also talk about --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And this is P156, Your Honours, the KLA Provisional Regulations For the Organisation of the Army's Internal Life, which you describe as being like a boy scout manual or scouting guide.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. And you stated that you didn't find anything. Well, you weren't aware of that until it was provided to you for this case; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you stated in your report: "Nowhere in it did I find any reference to the laws of war or to any form of court-martial nor any means of enforcing any form of discipline."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. In any meaningful way, we might add.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, you'll -- I don't want to go through this whole document, but do you recall reading from it that it talks about the need, for example, for discipline and order, Chapter 5, 2, "Obedience, respect and orders, strictly follow the Chamber chain of the military hierarchy."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They hadn't got a military hierarchy. And they're talking about doing it. But nowhere is it laid down as to how it's to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We're talking about the manual, the manual --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about aspirations. We're talking about an army which wants to be an army, desperately wants to be an army, but in the time it's got available to itself can't turn itself into an army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Listen to the question. My point is that type of language appears several times in the manual, the need for discipline. It talks about iron discipline.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aspirational language.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That language appears in the manual.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you look at Chapter 8, it -- and I can give you a copy of it or maybe we can -- sorry, it should be up on Sanction. I'll give you a hard copy. It talks about the military police and its duties. Point 3 states -- point 1 states, referring to the military police: "It is organised and protect servicemen and civilians in the territory of Kosovo, supervising and regulating traffic, pursuing and detecting those who commit military and civilian criminal acts." I'll give you a chance to read all this when it's brought to you. Point 3: "The military police is organised in operational zones and subzones to keep order and discipline in military units and bases in inhabited areas and other facilities of special importance." On the next page --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, which page are we on?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: These don't have page numbers. It's -- if you look towards -- it's the last two pages or so. It's Chapter 8.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My chapter 8 appears to be "Regulations for Health and Hygiene."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can I just see what you've been given?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chapter 6, "Duties of Responsible Persons."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I've got it for you here, sir. Okay. Do you have Chapter 8 now, "The Military Police and Its Duties"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that they do not have the said document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you could read the portions that I've read to you, which were in Sections 1 and 3. And then on the following page, among the duties of the police: "To seize the documents and weapons of servicemen and soldiers who break regulations and to escort them to the appointed place. All those who commit crimes are sent to the relevant organs with general notes relating to them." Now, did you read that when you reviewed this document for your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you think that's consistent with your report that "this is a boy scout for manuals [sic] without any means shown in it of enforcing any form of discipline, no means at all of enforcing discipline?"

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no means here, are there? This is an aspirational document to be sent to the relevant organs. What are the relevant organs? Where are they? Who commands them? Who controls them?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, you don't say that in your report. What you say in your report is that you're describing the manual. You describe the manual on Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. paragraph 36 as a "very nonmilitary manual. The manual seems mainly devoted to form and to aspects of personal life and so on, very much along the lines of a boy scouts manual. Nowhere in it did it find any reference to the laws of war or to any form of court-martial nor any means of enforcing any form of discipline."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the lines you've just described to me have nothing to do with enforcing discipline. It's an aspirational document that the military police should do this in a well-ordered world.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But we talked about -- you don't state that your report, this is an aspirational document, that it has references to mechanisms of enforcing discipline. Your report is not very accurate concerning this document, is it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this -- this document I looked at and I thought, We've no evidence to the distribution of this document. I've seen a claim that it must have been read to people. Well, it would have taken an awful long time to read to people. Outside of that, where does it come from? Who had it? Who did it go to? I wasn't aware of it before and frankly I didn't take I want very seriously. This is something which somebody produced in Pristina, by the look of it, as -- as I said, an aspirational document. It's all part of the same thing of wanting to become an army. But what we're examining is whether they managed to be an army with these functions in this time frame and to which my answer is no, they didn't, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Again, that is not what you're talking about in paragraph 36. You're describing the manual. But I'll continue. Just -- you would agree with me that disarming and arresting persons who commit military crimes and sending them to the appropriate organs is describing a way of enforcing discipline?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we knew what the appropriate or relevant organ was, yes. But as I said, this -- this starts with an idea, doesn't it? It's where we would like to be and where we would like to go. But it is not describing something which we know happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You talked a little bit about your background yesterday and that you didn't go to law school. I think you'd agree with me that somebody educated at Stanford Law School, who was Stanford's public interest lawyer of the year in 2004 and has spent his legal career working in the field in human rights is more qualified than you to comment on legal, jurisdictional issues. And there is an objection, so I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. I'm afraid I don't -- I do object to that. That's not a proper question for an expert to comment on somebody's ability or inability based on qualifications. So I don't see the relevance of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's a matter for submission, if I might say, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. We have about 10 minutes, Mr. Mansfield. Would that be profitable or would you think an early break better?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I think it would be profitable. I can't finish what I have to re-examine you about, but we can make a start on just a few of the topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: The first question I have for you -- and remembering the gaps, so I'll go slowly. Having listened -- having listened to all the questions and materials put to you, is there anything that has been put to you or any question that's been put to you that has caused you in any way to modify your opinion about the absence of an armed conflict in the relevant period in 1998?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: On a number of occasions, you've indicated, dealing with the lack of a command structure, that there was no effective structure in place. Would you kindly in summary form indicate what the components would be of a basic, not sophisticated -- of a basic, effective, military command structure that would qualify as such.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think to some extent at the very basic level you can see that in the NLA in Macedonia, where you have some form of central command structure, a commander, a deputy, a chief of staff who we know about commanding a number of defined brigades who were visible from the start of the conflict, who are in turn commanding sub-units. It doesn't really matter whether they're termed "battalions" or something else because these brigades, are actually only about the size of battalions. But -- commanding-defined sub-units, and with the clear ability to transmit orders. And we saw that in Macedonia, which was after this conflict, where the commander, Alija Ahmeti could order a withdrawal on two occasions, one of which we know was opposed by his chief of staff but nevertheless the withdrawals took place, and that was then in turn confirmed by the international community. Those actions were in support of a defined political objective and was using a military system of command to support those political objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, within -- within that answer, you've indicated one factor, the communication of orders. I just want to deal with other facets that you've mentioned, some this afternoon: staffing levels, knowledge, transportation. How are these to be considered within this structure?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: A military command structure needs a staff because without a staff you can't implement the commander's orders. And that started to develop within the KLA right at the end, when Ceku [Realtime transcript read in error: "Celiku"] came in and various subdivisions between supplies or logistics -- one of the people who has to be appointed is somebody in charge of military discipline, and there has to be a system of transmitting knowledge out through which people have to be known what they're supposed to be doing. You have to, as you said, you have to have transportation of some sort in order to move things around or you have to have an effective radio system. In Macedonia they continued to use the mobile phone system, which provided an excellent way of transmitting orders. And, of course, overall you have to have a way of imposing discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'm sorry to pause. I think there's been a misinterpretation. It is at line -- page 74, line -- sorry, line 18. The word "Celiku" has been mistakenly put in when, in fact, if you just read it, you were not --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ceku.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, Ceku. So if that could be changed in due course. Now, in the context of that answer, how do you regard, as the Prosecution finally conceded in their question, someone like Selimi claiming that he didn't know how his orders were communicated?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it as a desire. I'm afraid the whole context of that interview at times was indicating a desire in some ways to please the questioner. I think when he said he didn't know how his orders were communicated, what he actually means is they weren't being communicated. Otherwise, a commander would have to know how his orders were communicated. Because one of the things he'd want to be absolutely certain of was if his orders had been communicated, that they'd been received, understood, and that somebody was going to comply with them. If he didn't know that, then he wasn't issuing orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, one final matter before the break, still concerned with Mr. Selimi. This comes in the examination of this witness here by Mr. Nicholls himself, dealing with the appointment of Mr. Selimi. And what he said -- it is, in fact -- I'll give a day later, but I've got the page number. It's 2173, at line 21. What he told Mr. Nicholls was that "When the unit [Realtime transcript read in error: "community"] commanders were rallied round himself, there was a member of the General Staff present when they elected me as commander of the Drenica Operational Zone." What do you say about that in the context of a command structure?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The election of people who were referred to as "commanders," as although they didn't have command abilities or functions in my cases, was common throughout the KLA, particularly in 1998 and indeed early 1999. Commanders are supposed to be appointed because if a commander can be elected, he can be unelected if he doesn't do very well, and that doesn't lead to a military system. You haven't got a military system when commanders are elected. It would result in a very difficult way, again, of imposing discipline, which means in turn you can't really impose discipline with elected commanders. So you've got a series of groups fighting by common intent; but again, you haven't got a command system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, would that be convenient?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will resume at ten minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, just while the shutters are going up, may I just indicate -- yes, it's line 25, page 75, where I quoted the evidence of Mr. Selimi. I think there's one word wrong, and it's probably my fault, and I will certainly take responsibility: "When community commanders were rallied." In fact it's -- on the transcript it reads: "When the unit commanders were rallied around himself, there was a member of the General Staff." So I make that correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Churcher, in your last answer, you were dealing with discipline and I want to ask a similar question as I did with regard to the command structure. So far as you're concerned, what are the basic elementary components of an effective system of military discipline? Again, I'm not asking about a sophisticated system, just a basic elementary system.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a start, I think it's very difficult to have any form of enforceable military system if you haven't got a state or a state-like entity behind the command structure. But assuming that it might be possible to have a system of military discipline by consent without any form of legal basis, then at the top of the structure on the General Staff or the General Command or whatever, you would need to have a person who was responsible for disciplinary matters, and at every level of command, even if somebody had joint responsibilities, somebody else would have to be responsible for that. And you would have to have a laid-down system of how you tried somebody, and at least in practice you would have to see that. And you would have to have a system of graduated punishments, so that if somebody did a little bit wrong, they would get some sort of punishment and if somebody did something very wrong, they'd get another sort of punishment. Without that, you're simply relying on people's innate desire to be involved. But that doesn't amount to a system of discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, you -- at the start of that answer, you had a caveat in the form of referring to "a state or a state-like support entity behind the command structure." Looking at the Balkans, did the situation in the -- in Kosovo differ markedly from the situation in other Balkan states in relation to insurgency and armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the conflicts of the dissolution of Yugoslavia or however we like to refer to those Balkan conflicts of the 1990s, every other conflict had a state or a state-like entity, but I mean in fact state, behind it. So when Bosnia decided to defend itself, it had a Bosnian government. It utilised the Territorial Defence forces as the basis of its defend even though they had been disarmed. There was a parallel structure grew up but they managed to use a system of military discipline to dissolve that power in Sarajevo at a later stage of the war. There was a state. However embryonic, however insufficient, however broken up. Whereas in Kosovo there was no state and there was no state-like entity. The nearest thing there was to a state-like entity might have been the structures of the LDK set up abroad. But the KLA did not relate to these structures. Indeed, the KLA was opposed to those structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, in that context, I'd like you to go back to a document is that you were shown. I'm not sure whether you still have a hard copy in front of you, but it links to that last answer. It is in fact the Prosecution Exhibit 230. I think you were handed a hard copy. It's an ECMM report which was cited to you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's gone back again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Oh, I'll pause while it's brought back. Now, I'm not going to go over the paragraphs which have already been put to you, one entitled "UCK territory" and another "Road infrastructure" but just looking down that page towards the bottom -- and it may be -- if it could be brought up on a monitor so others can follow. I just want to go through this paragraph, "UCK membership."

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'm very grateful. It will just be slightly easier this way since not everybody's got it. It's the last paragraph entitled "UCK membership." I think that's legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I think it may be quicker if I just read it and if you'd kindly listen and then I'm obviously going to ask you for any further observations in the light of the answers you've given. And I'll go slowly, as it's being interpreted. "UCK membership. Throughout the past week the team has encountered probably more UCK" -- I think it should be "at checkpoints than Serb, and has been greeted by all sorts of individuals from local villagers carrying shotguns to masked UCK declaring themselves as leaders. The gradation of UCK member that we had previously suspected seems correct, with numerous villagers carrying weapons and even boys helping with the construction of trenches. But uniformed membership seems more substantial than first envisaged and is probably the result of more recent recruiting following the expansion of UCK-held territory. The hard core of" -- sorry -- "the hard core UCK membership appear almost invariably to have emerged from the diaspora, with a significant number from Germany, Austria, and Switzerland. They are confident and driven and occasionally nervous but nearly always courteous. It seems they are not aware of ECMM and so far have not wished to take advantage of our presence to communicate their wishes, indeed the overall impression is that they care little for the international community whom they distrust. And whilst NATO airstrikes might be convenient for them, they have no intention of waiting for them. The larger family unit to [sic] which an Albanian so often derives support is still the most plausible overall structure onto which the UCK is attached and will remain their greatest strength. In this way, membership of the UCK becomes unlimited." Now, I've taken a little time to read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me. No objection. I just believe the first line states "more UCK checkpoints" but it's not a mistake, that it should say "UCK at checkpoints." That make a difference --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- whether it's talking about the number of soldiers or the number of checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that, and I'd misread it. I thought it was "at checkpoints." Yes, I accept that. "Were UCK checkpoints than Serb." Yes. And having read that through, does that assist in the assessments and opinions you've given or not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that confirms what I was saying about the very diverse nature of the KLA as it started up, which relied on people who knew each other. And as you say, in particular, through the family connections, because that was who they trusted. Trust at that time was very difficult. There had been a number of false starts in the early 1990s where people had been betrayed and they were deeply suspicious, and therefore they returned to the wider family unit, to nephews and so forth, for connections. But the whole point about this is once again there's no military structure to it. There's a whole series of groups with different relationships, different connections. They don't know who each other are. People arrive in an area and start patrolling it only to discover some weeks later that unknown to them there are actually a whole series of self-appointed groups also patrolling the same area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Thank you. We can remove it from the monitor and pass to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: You will recall in the recent questioning there was confusion in the questions between two places, Racak and Rahovec. And I want to deal with the latter, Rahovec. And Mr. Limaj's evidence was quoted to you. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: This afternoon? Well, a little later -- in fact, it's a few paragraphs later, from the passage which was quoted, which concerned the fact that representatives of the General Staff were revealing that they'd only heard for the first time about the events at 7.00 or 8.00 in the morning, namely, at a much later -- well, at a later stage. Now, what Fatmir Limaj went on to say about this is -- and so it's clear, it's Day 69, and it's line 22, in which -- and it's page 68. Page 68, line 22, Day 69. He's been talking about a makeshift hospital, and then he says: "This happened in Rahovec. And if there is a mark about this period regarding the KLA, I think it's -- if there is is black stain, it's this because nobody knows how things really developed. This is one of the reasons I wanted to mention this, because I know this incident as a black stain that made the KLA pay a high price, both in casualties in its ranks and waivered people's confidence. Rahovec states or purely mirrors the way the KLA organised -- was organised at that time. It's a concrete example." Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I would disagree with there is, of course, the KLA was not organised, and that is precisely why Rahovec happened entirely accidentally. As we now know, a number of young men went back into the town carrying arms to visit their families. They collided with some Serbs. Fighting developed. People went to assist. And before the KLA knew it, they'd taken Rahovec, but they couldn't hold it. And "disaster" is too strong a word, but it was certainly a series public relations failure in the sense that the outside world thought they'd intended to take a town and then thought that they'd lost it, whereas in fact of course they hadn't intended to take it at all in the first place. And, of course, it was a personal disaster for a number of young men and villagers who went there to assist things and, I'm afraid, got killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: A further topic: If you could take up the bundle that you were provided with overnight by the Prosecution, tab 2. Contained within tab 2 is the letter headed "Southern Balkan consultants" with your name at the top. I just wanted -- if you'd just turn that up, headed "The Solution for Kosovo Independence." Could you indicate -- you've given a -- a brief context, why this letter was written both in its original form and in this form.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In its original form, it was written whilst I was in ICG as a support to a small book which was released suggesting conditional independence as a way out of the Kosovo problem, which would have been back in 2002. And then I was e-mailed, I think, by Shirley DioGuardi and asked to provide testimony to Congress and I pulled out that particular text, slightly revamped it, and sent it to her. I'm afraid that I didn't actually know that it was going to be used in this form or -- or appear in this form, but that was the intention behind it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And the book that -- to which it was lending support suggesting conditional independence, the book was being written or produced by people you knew or ...?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These were some pretty senior international political figures, High Minister of Sweden and senior figures in the US administration and so forth, who got together to suggest a course of action as a way out of the fact that the UN administration appeared likely to go on forever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, no more questions on -- on that document. I want, if I may, just finally to confirm through you so that it's clear, because you were asked about it yesterday, that you -- in order to compile the report, you were provided with a number of documents at different stages. And in particular, were you provided or have you been provided with transcripts emanating from this Tribunal from time to time for you to consider?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Quite a large number.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite a large number, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And also have you been provided with a correlation, as far as possible, of every single armed-conflict reference on transcript that could be -- as well as those other transcripts of evidence, that could be found?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not very recently, but perhaps a month ago I was provided with one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, finally this: I obviously would like, with Their Honours' permission, to exhibit your report. But before I do, is there any other matter that you feel you would like to add or subtract from anything that you've said so far?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I need to emphasise what I've said so far that if somebody is in difficulty about what could be regarded as effective military command, then I think the NLA in the Macedonia conflict demonstrates some aspects of that, a clear ability to transmit orders and to advance or withdraw on a set plan and set of orders which I, with hindsight, should have put in my own report but I was tending to look backwards for comparisons, and not forwards. But otherwise, no; I believe my report should stand as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if, in fact, now I could ask for his report to be exhibited. It would become DL12. I don't think there's any objection to that. And attached to it marked for -- in the way that -- the same way that has been done with other documents, that's Mr. Thaqi's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Mansfield, the investigator's notes of Hashim Thaqi's interview --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- of 2004 which were the subject of yesterday's deliberations is marked for identification as DL12.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'm sorry, right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we may not have allowed time for that to be announced yesterday. So that this report will be received and marked as Exhibit DL13, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be DL13, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That includes the CV, does it, Mr. Mansfield?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, it does. Yes. And it remains finally for me, if I may, just to thank Mr. Churcher for his patience, for Prosecution for allowing us to interpose him, and Your Honours also for allowing that slight deviation of the usual procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mansfield. Questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Churcher. I wonder if you could clarify a small matter for me. We've heard that you were the director of the International Crisis Group, I believe, from September 2000 till August 2001.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't actually become the director in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: I think that's what your CV says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in title. I think I became the -- I was there. I took over in November, as far as I remember. There was a period of handover.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Okay. And we have noted in the report no reference to any ICG report on the matter of KLA, its organisation, and development. That's correct? There isn't any? That's my clarification.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in my report, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: And is -- to your knowledge, has there after your tenure, as it were, at the ICG been produced any ICG report on KLA?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were reports produced before my tenure. As you're possibly aware, ICG reports are anonymous. I was aware of who'd written them. But with hindsight, they didn't really provide a very good picture, in my opinion, although, as I said, that's with hindsight. At the time, they were producing the best they could on very limited information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: But there were -- were reports on KLA under the label of ICG before --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not on the KLA, no. They were reports on the whole Kosovo situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You'll be pleased to know, Mr. Churcher, you may now leave. And I know you're pressed for time and must be free this evening, and we've managed to do that. Thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think if Mr. Limaj could now return to the witness box.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As you know, Mr. Limaj, the affirmation you took at the beginning of your evidence still applies. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, I would like to take up where we left off yesterday. When we -- when we stopped, I put to you the question about crimes in Lapusnik. I'd like to put the question to you more broadly. The question is this: To your knowledge, Mr. Limaj, during 1998 did the KLA - and when I say "KLA" I mean any soldiers of the KLA - did the KLA ever detain Serb civilians, to your knowledge, during 1998?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, Mr. Prosecutor, there might have been such cases that have happened in various areas of Kosovo, but you have to keep in mind that information at the time was very limited and I couldn't follow all the developments in all the areas. But such things could have happened, things that have been done in the name of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of any specific cases during 1998? Or are you just speculating?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke generally. There is a specific case, Your Honours. For example, in my brigade, we stopped two journalists - this is a concrete example that has to do with us - the two journalists that were stopped, the Tanjug journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We're going to talk about that a little bit later. Can you think of any other examples during 1998? Are you aware of any other examples?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally I don't know any concrete examples, but things have been said and I have heard, especially after the developments in Rahovec. Things were said about Serbs, especially the Serb media spoke about these things. At that time, we could not follow all the developments because the offensive was going on. But the Serbian citizens were speaking about these things and the Serbian media. But except that case that I mentioned to you that I knew directly, I did not know of any other concrete examples. I can't say now. I can't speak now of any other concrete examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did the Albanian media ever talk about such things?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
