utterances.text: To speak the truth, as I said, at that time it was almost impossible to communicate with the media at the time because of the situation. The media did not come. Sometimes Albanian media could penetrate and come to us. But, in fact, there was a lot of propaganda going on, both on the Albanian side and the Serb side. So I don't know for sure. I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall any instance -- you -- you specifically mentioned the Serbian media talking about these things. Do you recall any specific instance of the Albanian media talking about such things?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There could have been a media body that used that -- in fact, only two newspapers existed at that time. Maybe they asked Albanians about things or there was an interview. For example, maybe Mr. Krasniqi spoke to the media about those things. But, Your Honours, if I'm not mistaken, during that day --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, aside from the example that you've just given of Mr. Krasniqi talking about such things - and some of that is in evidence - can you think of any other specific examples of the Albanian media talking about such things? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember any specific cases. It might be -- it could be possible that there were reports, but I can't think of any now. I can mention here a case. Maybe it's of interest?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what it is, so I can't say if it's of interest.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you asked about the information I had -- Your Honours, Mr. Demaqi was appointed as a representative and also the International Red Cross sent names of people -- of Serbs who had disappeared or people that the Red Cross thought that they had disappeared. Maybe they communicated with the media. So that's what I wanted to say. There were Serbs who were -- were missing at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, I was going to ask about that later but I'll ask about it now, since you've brought it up. I -- there's evidence in the case that that list that you're referring to was provided by Mr. Demaqi to the General Staff in 1998 and that it was then distributed by the General Staff to zone commanders. Did you at that time -- according to your testimony, you were the commander of the 121 Brigade. Was the list distributed to you? Did you receive that list?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time, I did not see such a list. I mentioned Demaqi because I heard it from the media that he had contacts with the International Red Cross and the International Red Cross gave him such a list. I think later this was discussed in January, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The -- the list, according to the evidence, was provided in September of 1998. Did you hear about it in September of 1998 in the media? I can show you the article that's in evidence, if that's ...

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying, Mr. Prosecutor, that I heard about this meeting of Mr. Demaqi and the list that he had from the International Red Cross, and this is what I heard from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: My question is: When did you hear about it? Did you hear about it when it took place in September of 1998?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know specifically. It could be September or October, during that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you discovered -- was that the first time you heard that there were Serbs missing in Kosovo, or had you heard that before?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Serbian media spoke about this every day, but there was so much propaganda by the regime, so even if there were true things in what they said, we had to take it with a grain of salt because we thought it was all propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it from the Serbian media before, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you think that the list provided by the ICRC was propaganda?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Once you heard about that list and once you heard about the missing Serbs, did you --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- yourself, Mr. Limaj, to see if there was anything about missing Serbs in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, you have to separate these things. I was speaking about Serb propaganda, which is one thing, and the ICRC list is another thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your answer was clear on that. My question now is -- though I would note that the interpretation wasn't picked up, but your answer was that you did not consider the ICRC list to be propaganda. My -- I moved on to another question, which is: Once you -- when you heard about that list of missing Serbs, did you in your brigade, Brigade 121, take any steps to see if there was any information in your brigade about those missing Serbs?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, we did not know who these missing people were. We heard about missing people, but we didn't know who specifically they meant. And secondly, the territory where my brigade was, it was Albanian territory. There were no Serbs there. And we did not know the names of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: By that time there, were no Serbs there; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no Serbs even before in that territory, in that region.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were never Serbs there, living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did Serbs ever travel through that territory on the roads?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, gentlemen, I don't know who travelled through those roads, whether they were Serbs or Albanians, but in the territory of my brigade no Serbs were living there, not before the war, not -- nor during the war, neither after the war. So our territory was Albanian. Outside the area, yes; there were Albanians and Serbs living together in different towns, but -- and they could have travelled through the territory. But I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You're not aware that Serbs would travel on the main roads to get from one city to another, for example, to go to Pristina or to go to Stimlje? You're not aware of that? I mean, you must have known that.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're after. Of course people travelled on those roads, but I don't know who those people were. It was a main road. But of course, you must remember that that road was under the Serb control for most of the time, so I don't know how many people and who those people were who travelled on that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, the road, the Pristina-Peja road was under KLA control from Lapusnik on in June and July of 1998; correct? That was under KLA control. There's no dispute about that, is there?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just getting back to my question, I understand -- my question about what, if anything, you did to find out about missing Serbs. I understand your answer to be nothing.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You've given us reasons for it, but you did not do anything. For those reasons, you didn't do anything; correct? You said because -- because your territory was all Albanian and you didn't know the names, you didn't do anything. Is that a fair summary of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it, Mr. Prosecutor. First you're speaking about July -- June and July, and then about September and October. In June and July there were -- there was no 121 Brigade. You must be clear about this. Then in August and September the situation was completely different. If you speak about June and July, the road was blocked in Lapusnik. If you speak about August, it was open.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: My question is --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I need to explain this. It -- we have to be clear about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: My question -- I'm sorry if I wasn't clear about the dates. I was going back to September or October 1998, when you learned about this list. And my question had been: What, if anything, did you do about it? And I understand your answer to be because your territory was all Albanian and because you did not know the names, you did not do anything. Is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer, Mr. Prosecutor, is that I heard about missing Serbs, that the ICRC had a list. Second, with regard to my actions, in my brigade there was no Serb family living in the territory before the war, during the war, and after the war. My -- there might have been people who went missing, but I did not have any such information. Practically I did not have that information. It's a different thing when you say you did nothing and another thing when you say we did not have information. I am telling you the situation was such that we did not receive information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, the -- when we started off, I put the question to you with respect to Serb civilians, and now I will put the question to you -- a different question to you, similar but different, which is: To your knowledge, during 1998 did the KLA - meaning KLA soldiers - ever mistreat or torture prisoners held by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor and Your Honours, I never heard such a thing at that time, that a soldier -- a KLA soldier has done such things. Personally I never heard about something like that. I am not excluding the possibility that such a thing might have happened, but I personally did not hear of any such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Finally, to your knowledge, did -- during 1998, did the KLA - meaning soldiers of the KLA - ever murder prisoners held by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, you should take into consideration I am talking only about the territory where I was -- such things never happened in the part where I was working. I have not heard about that. As to what the KLA may have done, the KLA was operating all over Kosova. They were -- it was impossible to communicate among us. There were many things which we found out after the war, even with respect to organisation. Everything was difficult for us to learn, especially after the August offensive. Here I am talking only about myself and the place where I served. Such things did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of it happening elsewhere, outside of the place you say you served?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible they may have occurred in some place, but I cannot give you any concrete example. There are [indiscernible] developments in 1998, but I cannot give you anything in real terms. I didn't see anything, didn't hear anything, because of our very limited possibilities to communicate. For a long time one brigade couldn't communicate to the adjacent brigade, 121 to 122, because of the forces, of the Serb forces. Let alone about other zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, during the summer of 1998, June and July of 1998, one of the pseudonyms that Shukri Buja used was Sokoli; is that correct? Sometimes referred to as Sokoli?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. His pseudonym was Gazetari. His unit was called Sokoli. I know that his pseudonym was Gazetari. His unit was called Sokoli.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When, then, was Commander Sokoli?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are talking about the same person -- because there were many pseudonyms, such -- similar pseudonyms. There is a Sokol who was in the Lapusnik gorge on the other side of the road when you go to Likovc, at the junction that we said. There is a unit there not at the Lapusnik gorge but in Krajkove. You pass Lapusnik and there is a neighbourhood when you go to Likovc. There was a Sokol there. He was killed in October or November, I think. I don't know his last name. Maybe his name was Sokoli, I don't know. But he had his own unit there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was he a commander?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to say, I was -- I passed through Likovc once because to go to Likovc you had to pass through his unit. He was as a sort of -- a unit commander with maybe about 20 soldiers under his command. And I think, if I'm not mistaken, he was killed in Poklek in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Aside from that occasion you just described when you passed through his area on the way to Likovc, did you have any other occasion to see him during June and July of 1998, this person that you have described?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each time I went to Likovc, I had necessarily to go through his area. There was no other way. The road passed through the village where he was located. You couldn't go to Likovc from any other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Aside from going through his village, did you have during June and July 1998, did you have any other interactions with him, dealings with him?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by "interaction," but every time I passed by, I stopped. I stayed for some time there. I remember an occasion when myself and someone else were going to Likovc to get some uniforms and on the way to Likovc there were lined-up soldiers taking an oath. Now I remember, Sokol. It was on the central road that goes to Likovc. The soldiers were lined up on the side of the road when they were taking an oath. It's an interesting fact that the oath that they had obtained in a written form, because they didn't have a written rule, one of the soldiers had written it on a notebook and he was trying to read it out to 20, 30 soldiers that were there. I had the rules with me in my car and I stopped there and I stayed there until they finished the oath ceremony and I gave a speech. Since I happened to be there, they asked me to say a few words, and that I did. And I continued on my way to Likovc. This happened on the way to Obrinje-Drenice area. I think that is one of these occasions. But as I said, I have stopped there to have a coffee or to smoke a cigarette. If he or someone else happened to be there -- if I had time, of course, on the way to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, is -- the part of Drenica which is to the north of the Peja-Pristina road sometimes referred to as lower Drenica and the part that is south that starts with the Berisha Mountains, is that sometimes referred to as "upper Drenica"?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes. But there is not any explicitly divided border. It depends how you look at it. Someone [as interpreted] includes the entire Lapusnik and the area near Baince, Krajkove, Kroimire, Damanek, Lapusnik is the upper Drenice, and the area from the railway, from -- that divides Obrinje, they call it lower Drenice. From Krajkove, Damanek, Vukovc, Lapusnik, this part is seen as the upper Drenica. But I cannot tell you for certain because it's an unconventional division, I would say. It's a popular division. There is a railway which divides the area and they say on that part of the railway and on this part of the railway. The railway passes through Obrinje to Drenoc and Logovc [as interpreted] and continues to Kosova plain. This must be it. They -- some people refer to the asphalt road. Some refer to the railway. It depends. I personally, I can't give you a very clear description of it because it is not a geographical division, as I said, or an administrative one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, I'm going to show you -- I'm going to show you Prosecution Exhibit P37. No, I'm sorry, it's P39. Mr. Limaj, this is a newspaper article in Bujku from 4th of July 1998 and it describes an oath ceremony and Commander Sokoli reported on the units and Commander Celiku reviewed the troops. And it's in Drenica e Eperme. Now, this is referring to an oath ceremony with Shukri Buja, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't know. It may be the Sokoli I am talking about. It may be the Shukri. I don't know. I know that Shukri's pseudonym was Gazetari. But to rid you of your dilemma, I know that I was and visited this Shukri. Maybe it is about the other Sokoli. I am telling you that I visited Shukri and together with the Jakup Krasniqi, who at the time was staying in Kroimire, Mr. Prosecutor, as a representative of the General Staff because his wife had a problem with her pregnancy. So, Your Honours, his wife had just given birth --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You're getting a little bit far afield from the question. My question was: Is this -- is this oath ceremony with Shukri Buja, and I understand your answer to be it could be, you're not sure. Is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am trying to clarify things. This interview is possible to refer to the Sokoli I mentioned or to the other person, but I am telling you that Shukri's pseudonym was Gazetari. But to make things clear, I have attended ceremonies also at Shukrija. But this case that you're referring to me, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think you've answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the -- we can take the document back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, do you -- speaking of Shukri Buja, do you remember meeting up with him a few days after the Lapusnik gorge fell on the 26th of July, 1998? Do you recall seeing him?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, following the Lapusnik gorge, we met Shukri Buja on a daily basis because there was no other place you could go other than in Klecke or any other.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You've answered my question.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So we met daily.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall him telling you that he had released a group of men from Lapusnik or he had allowed -- he had stopped them and allowed -- and then allowed them to continue on their way? Do you recall him telling you that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember it, and I think what you are saying, it's not true at all. The population used to move from one place to another, but what you are putting to me is not true. He's never told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm not -- I'm just asking you questions. So you're -- are you saying that -- that you don't remember him talking to you about people coming from Lapusnik -- wait till I've finished the question. You don't remember it or it did not happen, that conversation?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, the population moved all about, from one place to another. Find accommodation. They went from one gorge to another, from one village to another. In this context, he may have said this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. But I -- I thought you were going off on a long answer again. If you can focus on the question. Do you remember having the conversation -- or are you saying that you didn't have the conversation or you don't remember having the conversation about men from Lapusnik with Shukri Buja?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to be brief. Such topics of people's movements were a common topic. But as to what you are asking me, I don't remember Shukri Buja to have told me anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, this conversation, just to press on a little bit further with this conversation, this conversation may have stood out because he indicated he was concerned about whether he had done the right thing in letting these people continue, which might have seemed out of the ordinary with respect to the context that you have described of refugees. Does that help you remember the conversation, the fact that he was concerned about having allowed these men from Lapusnik to continue?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You're shaking your head. You still don't remember?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. There were no such conversations. No, not the ones that you are referring to. With me, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, I'm going to move on to another topic, which is Rahovec. Now, as I understand your testimony, you arrived to a crossroads outside of -- of Rahovec at approximately 11.30 on July 17th, 11.30 at night. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I think so. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You stayed there through the night, through the day on the 18th, into the night of the 18th. At approximately 4.00 in the morning on the morning of the 19th, you had an encounter with a Serb soldier. You bumped into a Serb soldier. You then slept for approximately an hour and a half; you then woke up and went to get some coffee, and then you fainted. Is that -- is that your testimony? I'm just trying to fix the time you were there.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to clarify something. I didn't bump into a Serb soldier. I said that we didn't know that the Serbs had taken a position there. The soldiers told me later when the attack started, the soldier told me that the Serbs had been positioned in that place. It's not that I had seen it with my eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm just --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The others are as you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that you -- when you fainted, it's approximately 6.00 in the morning on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What time -- what time do you think it was in the morning? Can you give your best approximation of what time it was in the morning when you fainted on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately? I am trying to explain and to be brief. In the morning of the 19th, it may have been 5.00, 6.00, or 7.00, when the dawn came, I went to the juncture that you mentioned and I saw Byslym and the other representatives of the General Staff. I returned again, Mr. Prosecutor, to that point, to the place I was before. And there I had a coffee. After I had a coffee, I went again back to consult with Agim about something. When I went there, there I fainted. This is more or less 8.00 or 9.00. I may not be exact about the time, but it was not 6.00. I'm certain about that. It might have been either 8.00 or 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or less. You have to take it approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did you see Isak Musliu?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have already told you and told his lawyer as well in that -- at that time I -- in this early morning, I was interested to see what was going on. He might have been there. But when I went there, I was very tired that morning, at 6.00 or 7.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So are you saying -- are you saying now --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My point is that I was interested to talk with the representatives of the General Staff. Isak and many other members might have been there, but I don't remember. On the second time, when I went there he must have been with a group of soldiers because then I fainted and I don't have a clear recollection of what happened. That's why I am telling that I am not certain about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Is it -- is it fair to say, then, that Isak Musliu -- you might have seen Isak Musliu in Rahovec on that day, on the 19th, but you're not certain about it, you don't have a clear recollection about it? Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that I was focussed on those people of the General Staff, and then I fainted. He may have been there, but I am not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And aside from that moment when you fainted and he might have been there, did you see him at any other time in Rahovec after you arrived there at approximately 11.30 on the night of the 17th? Or is it -- is it the same answer, that you cannot recall?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about the 17th?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll rephrase my question. As I understand your testimony now, that you may have seen him on the morning of the 19th but you're not -- you don't have a clear recollection of it. Before the morning of the 19th, did you see him at Rahovec? Or is it the same --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you testified - and it's been referred to by your lawyer again today - that Rahovec was a black stain. And what you said is, "It's a black stain that made the KLA pay a high price both in casualties in its ranks and in -- and waivered people's confidence." Do you recall that testimony, Mr. Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes? You nodded your head but you didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Was Rahovec a black stain for another reason, Mr. Limaj? Is it a black stain for another reason?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. The consequences were very major. The black stain applies to all respects.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In what other respects was it a black stain -- is it a black stain?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to what I already stated, that various units of the KLA had -- had been involved in that adventure, in my opinion, a serious adventure which led to deaths of the members of the KLA and some civilians as well, there were -- I can't say hundreds. Maybe now I can't speculate with the numbers, but there were many civilians. They were saying thousands at that time. They were alleging there were thousands of civilians who are killed, violated, a bloodshed was committed there. This is what they were saying after the Serb forces entered. When things became clearer, it appeared that in addition to hundreds of Albanians there were Serb civilians killed as well or kidnapped, as the Serbs alleged. So for these too Rahovec is a black stain. There is no dilemma about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, you finally at the end of that long answer made reference to Serb civilians who were killed as well or kidnapped, and then you add "as the Serbs alleged." Do you have any doubt, Mr. Limaj, that more than 40 Serb civilians were kidnapped from Rahovec during that weekend and have never been seen again? Do you have any doubt about that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. You don't have in front of you a person who can behave towards the victims in this way. You are misinterpreting my answer. I do not be linked [as interpreted] to a people that can do such things. If you ask me questions, don't misinterpret my answers or don't give answers instead of myself. I can give the answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But I'm asking you to give the answers, and I give you every opportunity to give the answer. Do you have any doubt that -- about that, Mr. Limaj? Because you said "as Serbs alleged." You added that. Do you have any doubt about it in your mind, that that happened?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to explain to Their Honours that thousands of people said that a bloodshed was committed, that thousands of Albanians were killed, but in fact there were not thousands who were killed. I'm talking both about Albanians and Serbs. This rumour spread that thousands of people were killed and that Rahovec was a bloodbath. But when things became clearer, when the Albanians found out their victims, the Serbs on their part - now I am referring to Serbian formation - they said that there are Serbs who were killed. Now, if you're asking me whether you are doubting that there were Serbs who were killed or kidnapped, I don't have doubts because these were informations that were certified later on by the International Red Cross and other information. I could doubt -- I could question Serb-provided information, but I couldn't doubt information certified by other international organisations. I am not Dragan Jasevic, who says that there were no massacres committed in Likoshan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll have more questions about this tomorrow, but it's 7.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll resume tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
